input.command:
cd /Users/suhaan/devenv/gap-recency
git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'MSG'
feat(retrieval): time-weighted ranking

A brain accumulates, and relevance alone has no opinion about age. A decision
recorded on the first day and one recorded last week rank identically, so the
older answer keeps surfacing long after the newer one superseded it. Brain had
retract and gc - ways to remove a fact - and nothing that simply preferred the
recent one.

mem0 documents theirs as a soft ranking bias and never a filter, with no model
in the path. That is the whole design here too, and it is why the gap had no
excuse: it is arithmetic over a timestamp, under the same zero-token constraint
the rest of retrieval already works under.

Three properties, each with a test:

  - A bias, never a filter. Nothing is dropped. The multiplier spans 0.3x to
    1.5x, so a match five times stronger still wins however old it is; recency
    only decides ties and near-ties.
  - Absence of a timestamp is not evidence of age. Classic history records
    carry no time and get exactly 1.0. Demoting a whole corpus for a property
    it never claimed would be the easy bug here.
  - Opt-in. Switching it on silently would reorder every existing caller's
    results for a reason they never asked about, and a retrieval order that
    shifts for unexplained reasons is worse than one that ignores time.

Facts carry UpdatedAt onto the result rather than CreatedAt: a fact revised
last week is current regardless of when it was first written, and revision is
exactly the signal this should follow.

A future timestamp is treated as a broken clock, not a very fresh record, and
clamps to age zero rather than minting a multiplier above the ceiling.

Proof: neutralising recencyMultiplier to always return 1.0 - which still
compiles - fails TestRecencyMultiplierHalvesTowardTheFloor and
TestRecencyReordersButNeverDrops.
MSG
git push -q -u origin feat/recency-decay && echo "  pushed"
gh pr create --repo entireio/entire-brain --base main --head feat/recency-decay \
 --title "feat(retrieval): time-weighted ranking" \
 --body "$(cat <<'BODY'
Gap 2 of 12. Brain had `retract` and `gc` — two ways to *remove* a fact — and
nothing that simply preferred the recent one.

mem0 documents theirs as **a soft ranking bias, never a filter**, with no model
in the path. That is why this gap had no excuse and is labelled REAL GAP: it is
arithmetic over a timestamp, under the same zero-token constraint the rest of
retrieval already works under.

## The design is three properties, each with a test

**A bias, never a filter.** Nothing is dropped. The multiplier spans 0.3x–1.5x,
so a match five times stronger still wins however old it is — recency only
decides ties and near-ties. `TestRecencyCannotOverwhelmRelevance` pins that
boundary deliberately.

**Absence of a timestamp is not evidence of age.** Classic history records carry
no time and get exactly `1.0`. Quietly demoting a whole corpus for a property it
never claimed is the easy bug here, so there is a test that a record with no
timestamp — and one with an unparseable timestamp — is treated as neutral rather
than old.

**Opt-in.** Turning it on silently would reorder every existing caller's results
for a reason they never asked about. `retrievalOptions.Recency` defaults to
false and the test asserts that default.

## Details worth knowing

- Facts carry **`UpdatedAt`**, not `CreatedAt`: a fact revised last week is
  current regardless of when it was first written, and revision is exactly the
  signal this should follow.
- A **future timestamp is a broken clock**, not a very fresh record — clamped to
  age zero rather than minting a multiplier above the ceiling.
- Half-life defaults to 90 days. That is a judgement, not a measurement, and the
  comment says so: long enough that a quarter-old decision reads as current,
  short enough that last year's does not.

## Verification

- 6 tests covering the curve, the neutral cases, ordering, the relevance
  boundary, determinism, and the opt-in default
- **Behavioural revert proof:** neutralising `recencyMultiplier` to always
  return `1.0` still compiles, and fails
  `TestRecencyMultiplierHalvesTowardTheFloor` and
  `TestRecencyReordersButNeverDrops`. Deleting the file would only be a compile
  error, which proves less, so the neutralisation is the proof that counts.
- `internal/cli` full package green (243s), `go vet` and `gofmt` clean
BODY
)" 2>&1 | tail -1

**2 of 12 done.** Gap #3, recency decay — **PR #304**.

The design is three properties, each with its own test: it's a **bias, never a filter** (0.3x–1.5x spread, so a match five times stronger still wins however old it is); **absence of a timestamp is not evidence of age** (classic history records carry no time and get exactly 1.0 — demoting a whole corpus for a property it never claimed is the easy bug here); and it's **opt-in**, because turning it on silently would reorder every existing caller's results for a reason they never asked about.

Facts weight on `UpdatedAt` rather than `CreatedAt` — a fact revised last week is current regardless of when it was authored. A future timestamp is treated as a broken clock and clamped, not trusted.

feat(facts): write durable facts out as plain Markdown files

Facts lived only inside the store, reachable through recall and the MCP tools
and nowhere else. That is fine until you want to do the obvious thing - grep
them, read one in an editor, diff two branches, paste a decision into a review
- and find the only way in is a program. supermemory mounts its container as a
filesystem for exactly this reason.

`entire brain facts files` writes one Markdown file per fact, laid out by
taxonomy path:

    constraints/retry/policy/fact-57e03e4afc22.md
    architecture/api/ports/fact-bb6ca55edfd2.md

Front matter carries id, kind, branch, status, origin, timestamps and the
provenance anchor - provenance is what separates a fact from an assertion, so
it belongs in the file and not only in the store. The fact sentence is last,
unindented and unwrapped, so `grep -rn` returns the sentence rather than
metadata. Verified by running it: grep finds the line, cat reads cleanly.

It is a projection, not a second source of truth. Written fresh each run,
nothing reads it back, and the command says so in its help. A format people
edit and a store a program owns will diverge; the honest version of this
feature names which direction is canonical instead of pretending to sync.

Retracted and superseded facts are excluded by default, behind --all: writing
them beside live ones would make a grep return things the brain no longer
believes.

One correction to my own work is worth recording. The sanitiser's comment
claimed it was what kept output inside the export directory. It is not.
Splitting the taxonomy on "." destroys ".." before a segment can exist -
strings.Split("..", ".") is three empty strings - and filepath.Join cleans
under the root. The containment test passes with the sanitiser removed
entirely, so both the comment and the test now say what they actually
establish: the sanitiser makes usable directory names, and containment is a
structural invariant guarded against a future change to splitting or joining.

 --body "$(cat <<'BODY'

the MCP tools and nowhere else. That is fine until you want to grep them, read
one in an editor, diff two branches, or paste a decision into a review, and
discover the only way in is a program. supermemory mounts its container as a
POSIX filesystem for exactly this reason.

```sh

```

```
brain-facts/constraints/upload/limits/fact-e07be9baabcc.md

```

```console
constraints/upload/limits/fact-e07be9baabcc.md:13:The upload endpoint rejects payloads over 25 MB.
```

That is the whole point, and it is verified by running it rather than asserted.

## Design

- **Taxonomy is the directory layout**, so `ls` and tab-completion follow the
  same structure `recall` does.
- **Front matter carries provenance.** Provenance is what separates a fact from
  an assertion; it belongs in the file, not only in the store.
- **The sentence is last, unindented, unwrapped** — so `grep -rn` returns the
  sentence rather than a metadata line.
- **Retracted and superseded excluded by default** (`--all` to include). A grep
  that returns things the brain no longer believes is worse than no grep.
- **A projection, not a second source of truth.** Rewritten each run, never read
  back, and the help says so. A format people edit and a store a program owns
  will diverge; the honest version names which direction is canonical instead of
  pretending to sync.

## A correction to my own work

The sanitiser's comment claimed it was what kept output inside the export
directory. **It is not**, and I only found that by trying to break it: the
containment test passed with the sanitiser removed entirely.

Splitting the taxonomy on `"."` destroys `..` before a segment can exist —
`strings.Split("..", ".")` is three empty strings, never `".."` — and
`filepath.Join` cleans under the root. So the `.`/`..` check is unreachable
today.

a structural invariant guarded against a future change to splitting or joining.

threat test it isn't.

# Mem0 Memory Object Structure

Based on the API documentation, a memory object returned by the get/list memories endpoint contains these fields:

**Core Fields:**
- `id` (string, UUID): "Unique memory identifier"
- `memory` (string): "The extracted memory fact"
- `created_at` (string, date-time): Timestamp of creation
- `updated_at` (string, date-time): Timestamp of last update

**Scoping Fields:**
- `user_id` (string, nullable): User association
- `agent_id` (string, nullable): Agent association
- `app_id` (string, nullable): App association
- `session_id` (string, nullable): Run/session association

**Metadata & Classification:**
- `metadata` (object, nullable): User-supplied custom data
- `categories` (array, nullable): Memory tags/classifications
- `structured_attributes` (object, nullable): "System-derived temporal breakdown"

**Additional Fields:**
- `expiration_date` (string, date, nullable): Visibility cutoff date
- `replaced_by` (string, nullable): ID of superseding memory
- `synthesized` (boolean): Whether memory was synthesized vs. directly extracted

**Example from docs:**
```json
{
  "id": "f4cbdb08-7062-4f3e-8eb2-9f5c80dfe64c",
  "memory": "Alex is planning a trip to San Francisco from July 1st to July 10th",
  "created_at": "2024-07-01T12:00:00Z",
  "updated_at": "2024-07-01T12:00:00Z",
  "expiration_date": null
}
```

package cli

import (
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"strings"
	"sync"
)

// securityToggleWarned dedups the unrecognized-value warning so a garbage env
// value cannot flood stderr (brainNoEgressMode runs on every agent/export check).
var securityToggleWarned sync.Map

func brainNoEgressMode() bool {
	return securityToggleEnabled("ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS") || securityToggleEnabled("ENTIRE_BRAIN_LOCAL_ONLY")
}

func envBool(name string) bool {
	switch strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(os.Getenv(name))) {
	case "1", "true", "yes", "on":
		return true
	default:
		return false
	}
}

// securityToggleEnabled reads a fail-closed security toggle. Canonical
// true/false values are honored and an unset/empty value is off (these guards are
// opt-in). Any other, unrecognized value is treated as ENABLED and a warning is
// emitted — so a typo'd "enabled"/"ture" can never silently leave a no-egress
// guard switched off, which would fail open to egress.
func securityToggleEnabled(name string) bool {
	raw := strings.TrimSpace(os.Getenv(name))
	switch strings.ToLower(raw) {
	case "", "0", "false", "no", "off", "disable", "disabled":
		return false
	case "1", "true", "yes", "on", "enable", "enabled":
		return true
	default:
		if _, seen := securityToggleWarned.LoadOrStore(name, struct{}{}); !seen {
			fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "warning: %s is not a recognized boolean; treating as enabled (fail-closed)\n", name)
		}
		return true
	}
}

// rejectAgentForNoEgress fails closed: under no-egress mode only agents that are
// known to stay on local loopback (ollama / none) are permitted. Any other value
// — including a newly-added or unknown agent name — is denied, so the guard
// cannot be bypassed by an agent the allowlist has not yet been taught about.
func rejectAgentForNoEgress(agent string) error {
	if !brainNoEgressMode() {
		return nil
	}
	switch strings.TrimSpace(agent) {
	case "ollama", "none", "":
		return nil
	default:
		return fmt.Errorf("no_egress: --agent %s can send selected brain context outside local loopback; use --agent ollama for local loopback models, --agent none where supported, or unset ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS/ENTIRE_BRAIN_LOCAL_ONLY", agent)
	}
}

plainly:

- **It reads sensitive material by design.** Repository source, agent session
  transcripts, prompts, commit history, and documentation.
- **It keeps that material on your machine.** The brain lives under the plugin
  data directory; `entire brain path` prints the location for a repository.
- **The default build makes no network calls.** `entire brain doctor` reports
  the effective egress policy under `memory_provider_egress`. Agent-dependent
  commands — `distill`, and anything invoking a hosted model — are the
  exceptions, and they are opt-in.

Because transcripts and source can carry credentials that were never meant to
be retained, Brain applies a redaction pass to synthesised evidence, rendered
cards, transcript excerpts, drafts, and JSON egress. It targets tokens, JWTs,
secret-shaped environment assignments, private-key blocks, and home-directory
paths.

**Treat that redaction as a mitigation, not a guarantee.** It is pattern-based
and cannot recognise every secret shape. A brain built from a repository whose
history contains real credentials should be handled with the same care as the
repository itself.

### Brain without fact extraction

Extracting facts uses an available agent CLI and can send session content to its model provider and incur token charges. Without an agent CLI, this step is skipped. 

To build without fact extraction or a background service, use:

```sh
entire brain setup --no-backfill --no-daemon
```

## Privacy And Egress

Default brain artifacts are local and inspectable. Deterministic refresh,
semantic indexing, local history indexing, and MCP tool calls do not require a

model or by fetching over the network:

  egress, not a hosted-model call, skipped under no-egress mode

- fact distillation with `distill --agent ...`
- query expansion with `recall --expand`

- explicitly configured session-abstract generation
- judged evaluation commands
- `publish` uploads the serialized local brain (manifest, semantic snapshots,
  branch overlays, durable facts) to hosted Entire; opt-in and off by default,
  requiring both the command and `ENTIRE_BRAIN_ALLOW_HOSTED=1`

import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("docs/reference.md"); s = p.read_text()
anchor = "## Privacy And Egress\n"
section = """## Webhooks

A brain's knowledge is only visible to whoever runs a command against it.
Webhooks let something else react instead: a CI job that re-runs when a new
invariant is recorded, a channel that shows decisions as they are made, an index
that rebuilds when the brain refreshes.

Point it at an endpoint and it is on:

```sh
export ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_URL=https://hooks.example.com/entire
export REDACTED   # recommended
entire brain webhook test        # prove the endpoint works before trusting it
entire brain webhook status      # what is on, and why it is off when it is
entire brain webhook events      # what this brain sends
```

Unset `ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_URL` and nothing is sent and no connection is made.
There is no config file and no default endpoint.

### Events

| Event | Sent when |
| --- | --- |
| `fact.recorded` | `remember` records a durable fact |
| `fact.retracted` | `facts retract` marks a fact no longer true |
| `brain.refreshed` | `refresh` completes |
| `webhook.test` | only by `webhook test` |

A `fact.recorded` POST looks like this:

```json
{
  "event": "fact.recorded",
  "timestamp": "2026-09-21T10:00:00Z",
  "repo": "entire-brain",
  "branch": "main",
  "fact": {
    "id": "b3f1c2d4",
    "kind": "invariant",
    "paths": ["architecture.storage.invariant"]
  }
}
```

### What is and is not sent

**Fact text is withheld by default.** The payload carries the id, kind and
taxonomy paths — enough to trigger work, not enough to turn one environment
variable into a feed of everything the brain has learned. Set
`ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_INCLUDE_TEXT=1` to add a `text` field when you want the
fact itself in your channel.

`repo` is the repository's directory name, never its path, so an event does not
disclose the layout of your filesystem.

### Verifying the sender

With `ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_SECRET` set, each POST carries
`X-Entire-Signature-256: sha256=<hex>`, the HMAC-SHA256 of the exact request
body. Compute the same over the raw body and compare in constant time:

```python
import hashlib, hmac
expected = "sha256=" + hmac.new(secret.encode(), raw_body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
if not hmac.compare_digest(expected, request.headers["X-Entire-Signature-256"]):
    abort(401)
```

Without a secret no signature header is sent at all, rather than one computed
over an empty key — which would verify for anyone who guessed the key was empty.

### Limits worth knowing

- **Redirects are refused, not followed.** A 307 preserves the method and body,
  so following one would deliver the payload and its signature to a host you did
  not configure. Point `ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_URL` at the final URL.
- **`http` and `https` only.** Other schemes are rejected.
- **Delivery never fails the command.** If the endpoint is down, the fact is
  still recorded and a warning goes to stderr. There is no retry queue: this is
  a notification channel, not a delivery guarantee. Treat a missed event as
  possible and re-read state through `/v1/facts` or the CLI when it matters.
- **`ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS` and `ENTIRE_BRAIN_LOCAL_ONLY` win.** Either one
  silences webhooks whatever else is configured.

"""
assert anchor in s
p.write_text(s.replace(anchor, section + anchor, 1))
print("reference section added")
PY

## Features

- Give an agent relevant decisions, code locations, and suggested tests before it starts a task.
- Save project facts by hand or extract them from past sessions, then check their source references against the repository.
- Search facts, history, documentation, and conversations by keyword or meaning.
- Find code, inspect the impact of a change, and investigate regressions with [Entire Graph](https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph).
- Connect agents through the CLI or MCP, with response size limits and repository instructions.
- Browse saved knowledge in a terminal dashboard or an offline graph view.
- Brain reads sessions captured by Entire CLI and uses Entire Graph for code analysis. Without captured sessions, Brain builds from code, docs, and Git history.
- Graph is required for code analysis, but you can use Brain to search sessions, docs, and facts without it.

=== 233,282 ===
### Recover from a split brain

A repository reached through two different paths — a symlink, or `/tmp` on
macOS — could once end up with two brains and then refuse every repo-scoped
command. Keys are now derived from the resolved directory, so new splits
cannot happen; if you have an existing one:

```bash
# List every store this repository resolves to.
entire brain repo-identity

# Keep one and retire the others (renamed to a dated sibling, never deleted).
entire brain repo-identity --keep <repo-key>
```

## Stored memory and freshness

Brain's code index can fall behind your working tree. The watcher updates it automatically; run `entire brain refresh` to update it manually. Graph's interactive queries normally read the current working tree directly.

Run `entire brain verify` to check whether a fact's source references still match the repository.

`entire brain path` prints where this repository's memory is stored. See [storage and configuration](docs/reference.md#storage-and-configuration) to change storage locations or search settings.

To stop and remove the watcher, run `entire brain setup --uninstall-daemon`. See [operations](docs/operations.md#after-the-install-onboard-a-repository) for service management.

## Limitations

Facts extracted by a model can be wrong. Check the linked sources before relying on them. `brain verify` checks source references, not whether a conclusion is correct.

Code analysis inherits Graph's limitations: dynamic calls can go unresolved, and parsing support varies by language.

Search support varies by build and source. Check `entire brain capabilities` for available retrieval modes and the [conversation recall documentation](docs/recall-evidence.md) for experimental features.

See the [recall threat model](docs/recall_threat_model.md) for how Brain handles untrusted session content and retained secrets.

# How Brain compares

`feature-matrix.csv` opens in Excel, Numbers or Sheets: 51 capabilities across
Entire Graph, Entire Brain, Graphify, mem0, cognee, supermemory and
codebase-memory-mcp.

## Two caveats

**Our columns are measured; the others are not.** Graph and Brain are read from
the shipped binaries — mostly `entire graph capabilities --json` and
`entire brain capabilities --json` — so you can reproduce them. The five
competitor columns come from public documentation. Nothing was installed or
benchmarked. Every claim about another product cites a page in `Source`, and
`Unknown` means unknown, never "no".

**We chose the rows.** The first version had 31 and Graph or Brain answered Yes
to all of them, which is what happens when the people who build the product pick
the questions. It now has 51, and **20 are rows where neither of ours answers
Yes**. Graph answers Yes to 19 of 51; Brain to 26, delegating 5 more to Graph —
counted separately, because delegating is not having.

## Labels in the Notes column

| label | meaning | rows |
|---|---|---|
| **REAL GAP** | We lack it, and local-only + zero-LLM does not explain why | 12 |
| **TRADE-OFF** | We lack it as a direct cost of that design | 5 |
| **PARTLY REAL** | Part of the absence is excused, part is not. Describes the verdict, not a partial capability — such a row can read `No` in both our columns | 2 |
| **THEY DO IT BETTER** | We demonstrably have it and someone goes further. Not used where our cells are `Unknown` | 2 |

## What the gaps say

"We are local" explains fewer absences than it appears. Three local-first tools
break that defence on their own: **codebase-memory-mcp** ships 162 languages
with an embedded language-server pass and no API keys against our 36 semantic of
185; **Pieces** stores everything on-device and still captures across every
application rather than one repository; **Graphify** parses PDFs, Office files
and live Postgres schemas with tree-sitter.

The sharpest gap is what an agent can write. Brain's MCP surface has 36 tools
and four write — `brain_index_repository`, `brain_refresh`,
`brain_ingest_traces`, `brain_delete_project` — all of them derived state. None
authors a durable fact, so an agent cannot record what it just learned;
`entire brain remember` is a CLI command.

## Tools cited without a column

`Notes` and `Source` sometimes cite Pieces, Letta, Zep, Serena, Augment, Zoekt,
Cursor, Sourcegraph, Copilot or Windsurf, where the best evidence came from
outside the five. They are named where relevant but not assessed across all 51
rows.

If you change one of our cells, cite the command. If you change a competitor
cell, cite the page. If a row only exists because it flatters us, delete it.

feat(webhooks): notify another service when the brain changes

A brain's knowledge was only visible to whoever ran a command against it.
Nothing could subscribe, so a CI job that should re-run when an invariant is
recorded, a channel that should show decisions, or an index that should rebuild
after a refresh all had to poll or go without.

`ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_URL` turns on three events — `fact.recorded`,
`fact.retracted`, `brain.refreshed` — plus `webhook.test` for proving an
endpoint works before trusting it. `entire brain webhook status` says whether
they are on and why not when they are off, because silence is the failure mode
webhooks have.

This is the only outbound traffic the default build makes, so the guards are
the substance of the change:

- Off until a URL is typed. No config file, no discovery, no default endpoint.
- `brainNoEgressMode()` outranks the configuration. A local-only declaration
  one subsystem can opt out of is not a declaration.
- Fact text is withheld unless `ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_INCLUDE_TEXT` is set, and
  that decision lives in `newFactWebhookEvent` so no call site can forget it.
  Events carry ids, kinds and paths; `repo` is the directory name, not a path
  that discloses a home directory's layout.
- Redirects are refused rather than followed. A 307 preserves method and body,
  so following one delivers the payload and its HMAC signature to a host nobody
  configured.
- `http`/`https` only.
- Delivery never fails the command. A fact is on disk before anything is
  notified, and an unreachable endpoint is a warning on stderr.

Each of those is pinned by a test checked against a weakened build: deleting
the egress gate, the scheme check, the redirect policy, the redaction, the
signature, or the error-status check each turns a test red, as does advertising
an event nothing emits. Verified end to end against a real listener that
recomputes the HMAC independently.

SECURITY.md's "the default build makes no network calls" now names webhooks
alongside the agent commands as the opt-in exception, rather than leaving the
sentence to imply this cannot exist.

gh pr create --repo entireio/entire-brain --base main --head feat/webhooks --title "feat(webhooks): notify another service when the brain changes" --body "$(cat <<'BODY'
Closes gap #9 on the feature matrix: *"Framework integrations and webhooks — REAL GAP. Packaging, not design. 20+ integrations versus our zero; mem0 has 8 webhook event types."*

## The problem

A brain's knowledge is only visible to whoever runs a command against it. Nothing could subscribe. A CI job that should re-run when a new invariant is recorded, a channel that should show decisions as they are made, an index that should rebuild after a refresh — all had to poll, or go without.

## What this adds

```sh
export ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_URL=https://hooks.example.com/entire
export REDACTED

entire brain webhook test     # prove the endpoint works before trusting it
entire brain webhook status   # what is on, and why it is off when it is
entire brain webhook events   # what this brain sends
```

| Event | Sent when |
| --- | --- |
| `fact.recorded` | `remember` records a durable fact |
| `fact.retracted` | `facts retract` marks a fact no longer true |
| `brain.refreshed` | `refresh` completes |
| `webhook.test` | only by `webhook test` |

Four events, not eight. Every name is emitted by real code, and a test fails if one is advertised and never sent — a list a consumer can subscribe to and receive nothing from is worse than a shorter list.

`status` exists because silence is the failure mode webhooks have: it distinguishes "never configured" from "configured but gated" from "configured but unusable", and the hint points at whichever knob is actually wrong.

## The guards are the substance

This is the only outbound traffic the default build makes, so most of the work is the conditions under which it makes none.

- **Off until a URL is typed.** No config file, no discovery, no default endpoint.
- **`brainNoEgressMode()` outranks the configuration.** `ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS` / `LOCAL_ONLY` silences webhooks whatever else is set, checked centrally rather than per call site. It inherits the fail-closed toggle parsing, so a typo'd `ture` disables egress rather than enabling it.
- **Fact text is withheld by default.** Events carry the id, kind and taxonomy paths. The decision lives in `newFactWebhookEvent`, so no call site can forget it; `ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_INCLUDE_TEXT=1` opts in. `repo` is the directory name, never the path.
- **Redirects are refused, not followed.** A 307 preserves method and body, so following one delivers the payload *and its HMAC signature* to a host nobody configured — the same shape as the auth-go redirect leak.
- **`http`/`https` only.** A `file://` "webhook" would make one env var a write primitive.
- **Delivery never fails the command.** The fact is on disk before anything is notified; an unreachable endpoint is a warning on stderr. No retry queue — this is a notification channel, not a delivery guarantee, and the docs say so.

## Verification

**Every guard was checked against a weakened build.** 15 weakenings applied one at a time; each turns a test red:

| weakening | caught by |
| --- | --- |
| egress gate deleted | 4 tests |
| scheme restriction removed | `TestWebhookRefusesNonHTTPSchemes` |
| fact text always included | 2 tests |
| full repo path sent | `TestFactWebhookWithholdsTextByDefault` |
| redirects followed | `TestWebhookRefusesToFollowRedirects` |
| 4xx/5xx treated as success | `TestWebhookTreatsAnErrorStatusAsAFailure` |
| signature dropped / over wrong bytes / sent without a secret | `TestWebhookSigns…`, `TestWebhookIsUnsigned…` |
| delivery failure propagated to `remember` | `TestRememberStillRecordsWhenTheWebhookEndpointIsDown` |
| `webhook test` no longer refuses when off | `TestWebhookTestRefusesWhenWebhooksAreOff` |
| event advertised but never emitted | `TestEveryAdvertisedEventIsActuallyEmitted` |
| event listed with no description | `TestWebhookEventsCommandDescribesEveryEvent` |

**End to end against a real listener** that recomputes the HMAC independently: `webhook.test`, `fact.recorded` and `fact.retracted` all delivered with `sig_verifies=True`, payloads carrying ids/kinds/paths and no fact text. The redirect, no-egress, fail-closed-typo and `file://` cases produced **zero** deliveries to the sink.

That live run found two real bugs the unit tests were too loose to catch, both fixed here with the tests tightened: `status` told users to set a URL they had already set when an egress toggle was the actual cause, and `file://` was reported as "not a valid URL" because the host check ran before the scheme check.

`go test ./...` 5341 pass · `go vet ./...` clean · `gofmt -l -s` clean · race clean.

python3 - <<'PY'
import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("docs/reference.md"); s = p.read_text()
anchor = "## Privacy And Egress\n"
section = """## Documents

Brain indexes markdown from `docs/` and, alongside it, the documents that are
not code: PDF, Word, Excel and PowerPoint. A design doc somebody wrote in Word
and a spec that arrived as a PDF are project knowledge exactly like a `.md`
file, and were previously invisible to every query.

```sh
entire brain docs formats                 # what this build reads
entire brain docs extract docs/spec.pdf   # the text it gets out of one file
entire brain docs extract docs/spec.pdf --json
```

Extraction runs during `refresh`, with the rest of the seed. It is fully
deterministic and local — no model, no network, no external binaries — so it
costs no tokens and works offline.

### What is read

| Format | Read | Not read |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.pdf` | the text layer, page by page | scans (no text layer), encrypted files |
| `.docx` | body, footnotes, endnotes; tables as tab-separated rows | headers and footers, which repeat on every page |
| `.xlsx` | every sheet, labelled with its own name; shared strings resolved | charts, formulas (the computed value is read) |
| `.pptx` | slides in deck order, then speaker notes | slide masters and layouts |

Legacy `.doc`, `.xls` and `.ppt` are a different format (OLE compound files),
not a variant of the above, and are not read. Images are not read: that needs
OCR, which would mean shipping a native dependency.

### Where they are read from

`docs/`, the same place markdown is taken from — not the whole tree. A `.xlsx`
under test fixtures or a vendored PDF manual is data rather than documentation,
and indexing those would bury the documents somebody meant to be read.

Extracted text is written into the brain as `seed/docs/<path>.md` with a header
naming the source, so it is inspectable as plain text and it is obvious the file
is derived. The original document is never modified.

### When a document cannot be read

Brain reports it and continues; the refresh still succeeds. The reason lands in
the seed's file index and in the refresh warnings:

```
warning: document not indexed: docs/scanned-form.pdf: the PDF has no text layer
  (it is probably a scan; OCR is out of scope for this build)
```

Nothing is written for that document. An empty markdown file in the seed would
be indexed as a document that exists and says nothing, which is worse than an
absence somebody can see.

Three failures are reported rather than guessed at, because each would otherwise
produce a plausible-looking result that is wrong:

- **A scan** has no text layer at all. Indexing it as an empty document would
  count as a successful ingest.
- **An encrypted PDF** cannot be read without its key.
- **A font this build cannot map.** Modern PDFs embed subset fonts whose bytes
  are glyph indices rather than characters; Brain decodes them through the
  font's `/ToUnicode` map, and where that is missing or unusable it refuses
  rather than emit text that reads like language and matches no query.

### Untrusted input

A document is untrusted input and is treated as such: file size, decompressed
size, and archive entry count are all capped before parsing starts, so a
compression bomb costs a bounded read. Extracted text is stripped of control
characters and is never executed or interpreted — it is indexed as text, and the
[recall threat model](recall_threat_model.md) covers how retrieved content is
handled from there.

"""
assert anchor in s
p.write_text(s.replace(anchor, section + anchor, 1))
print("reference updated")
PY

feat(docs): read PDF, Word, Excel and PowerPoint into the brain

Brain indexed markdown and nothing else. The design doc somebody wrote in Word,
the spec that arrived as a PDF, the requirements matrix in a spreadsheet — all
invisible to every query, even sitting in `docs/` beside the files it did read.
"We run locally" never explained it: these are container formats with
deterministic parsers, they cost no tokens, and Graphify parses the same set
on-device.

Extraction is standard library only. Office files are ZIP archives of XML, which
`archive/zip` and `encoding/xml` read completely; PDF text needs `compress/zlib`
and a small object parser. No new module dependencies, because the install
instructions promise no Go toolchain and no C compiler and a reader that needed
libxml or tesseract would quietly make them false.

The hard part is not parsing, it is refusing to produce plausible garbage.
Modern PDFs embed subset fonts whose string bytes are glyph indices, not
characters, so naive extraction yields fluent-looking rubbish that fills the
index with text no query can match and no reader can recognise as broken. So:
each font's /ToUnicode CMap is resolved and decoded through, an unmappable
composite font emits nothing rather than its glyph bytes, and a final gate
rejects output that does not read as language. Three failures are reported
rather than guessed at — a scan has no text layer and needs OCR, an encrypted
file cannot be read, and an unmappable font is not text.

Documents are read from `docs/`, the same place markdown is taken from, and
land as `seed/docs/<path>.md` with a header naming the source — so the text is
inspectable, obviously derived, and reachable by the doc indexer, which only
walks markdown. A document that cannot be read is named in the refresh warnings
and writes nothing, because an empty markdown file in the seed would be indexed
as a document that exists and says nothing.

`entire brain docs extract <file>` and `docs formats` answer "will this be read,
and as what" without running a refresh and reading the brain directory after.

extracted, and every one of the 4 refusals is a genuine scan (all declare zero
fonts). That run found two defects a fixture suite would not have — a ligature
the producer omitted from its own CMap being emitted as a stray "(", and the
whole-document fallback path re-emitting glyph bytes the page path had
deliberately withheld. Both fixed. End to end, text that exists only inside a
PDF and only inside a spreadsheet now comes back from `brain search` citing the
source document.

21 weakenings were applied one at a time and each turns a test red, including
the four that initially did not: a table whose rows collapsed to one cell per
line, a prose gate tested only as a predicate and never through the entry point,
a zip-bomb fixture that yielded no text either way, and a PDF fixture small
enough to survive a truncated prefix read.

## The problem

Brain indexed markdown and nothing else. A design doc written in Word, a spec that arrived as a PDF, a requirements matrix in a spreadsheet — all invisible to every query, even sitting in `docs/` beside the files it did read.

## What this adds

```sh
entire brain docs formats                  # what this build reads
entire brain docs extract docs/spec.pdf    # what it gets out of one file
```

Put a PDF or Office file in `docs/` and `refresh` reads it into the brain alongside markdown.

| Format | Read | Not read |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.pdf` | text layer, page by page | scans, encrypted files |
| `.docx` | body, footnotes, endnotes; tables as rows | headers/footers (they repeat on every page) |
| `.xlsx` | every sheet, labelled with its name; shared strings resolved | charts |
| `.pptx` | slides in deck order, then notes | masters and layouts |

**Standard library only — no new module dependencies.** Office files are ZIP+XML, which `archive/zip` and `encoding/xml` read completely; PDF needs `compress/zlib` and a small object parser. The install instructions promise no Go toolchain and no C compiler, and a reader that needed libxml or tesseract would quietly make them false.

## The hard part is refusing to produce plausible garbage

An extractor has two ways to fail and only one of them is visible. It can refuse a document it should have read — somebody notices. Or it can return text that looks fine and is wrong, which nobody notices until a search quietly stops finding things.

Modern PDFs embed subset fonts whose string bytes are **glyph indices, not characters**. Naive extraction yields fluent-looking rubbish. So:

- each font's `/ToUnicode` CMap is resolved and decoded through (`bfchar` and `bfrange`);
- a composite font with no usable map emits **nothing** rather than its glyph bytes;
- a final gate rejects output that does not read as language.

Three failures are reported rather than guessed at, each because the alternative is a convincing wrong answer:

```
docs/scanned-form.pdf: the PDF has no text layer
  (it is probably a scan; OCR is out of scope for this build)
```

## Verification

**Against 25 real documents on this machine, not only synthetic fixtures.** 21 extracted; all 4 refusals are genuine scans — independently confirmed, every one declares **zero fonts** and is a wall of DCTDecode/CCITTFax images.

That run found two defects a fixture suite would never have surfaced:

1. A ligature the producer omitted from its own CMap was being emitted as a stray `(` — "Cover Le(er". Unmapped codes in a font that *has* a map are glyph indices, so they are now dropped rather than passed through.
2. **The whole-document fallback path re-emitted the glyph bytes the page path had deliberately withheld.** The page path correctly returned nothing for an unmappable font, the fallback then ran and undid it. This is the exact mojibake the design exists to prevent, arriving through the back door.

**End to end**, through the real binary and a real `refresh`: text existing *only* inside a PDF and *only* inside an `.xlsx` comes back from `brain search`, citing the source document and line.

**21 weakenings applied one at a time, each turns a test red** — ToUnicode ignored, bfrange not advancing, kern threshold removed or made universal, only-first-content-stream, encryption undetected, prose gate removed, namespace-prefix matching, shared strings ignored, slides sorted lexically, zip caps removed, documents selected from the whole tree, container read as a prefix, and more.

Four of those initially **did not** fail, and fixing that found real bugs:

| test that could not fail | what it was hiding |
| --- | --- |
| table cells | rows collapsed to one cell per line — a label separated from its value is not a table |
| prose gate | tested as a predicate, never through the entry point |
| zip bomb | fixture yielded no text either way, so the cap was untested |
| prefix read | PDF fixture small enough to survive truncation |

- **Scoped to `docs/`**, the same place markdown is taken from. A `.xlsx` under test fixtures or a vendored PDF manual is data, not documentation, and indexing those would bury the documents somebody meant to be read. There is a test that a PDF outside `docs/` does *not* bypass the binary checks.
- **Images are not read.** That needs OCR, which means a native dependency. Said plainly in the docs and in `docs formats` rather than left as a silent gap.
- Legacy `.doc`/`.xls`/`.ppt` are OLE compound files — a different format, not a variant — and are declined by name.

Global facts are recalled from every repository and labelled `(global)` when
they surface, so a general convention is never mistaken for something this
codebase declared. `--no-global`, or `ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_GLOBAL_FACTS=1`, leaves

anchor2 = "## Privacy And Egress\n"
section2 = """## Global Facts

A fact normally belongs to a repository and a branch. That is right for a claim
about one codebase and wrong for the rest: "I prefer table-driven tests", "we
deploy on Thursdays", "the staging cluster is in eu-west-1" are true everywhere,
and recording them in one repo's brain makes them invisible from the next.

```sh
entire brain remember "We deploy on Thursdays." --global
entire brain facts global                     # list them
entire brain facts global --all --json
entire brain facts retract <fact-id> --global
```

Global facts live in their own store beside the per-repo ones — `global/` next
to `repos/` under the plugin data directory, which `entire brain facts global`
prints. They are ordinary facts: the same format, the same taxonomy, the same
retraction and garbage collection.

### How they surface

`recall` merges them into every repository's results. They go through the same
filters and ranking as repository facts, and are labelled:

```
fact:76aa6fd6 decision [architecture.deployment.convention] (global)
  The staging cluster is in eu-west-1.
```

The label matters: acting on a general convention as though this repository had
declared it is a different thing, and an agent reading unlabelled output cannot
tell the difference. `--json` reports the same distinction as `global_fact_ids`.

Where a repository records the same statement, the repository's copy wins —
fact ids are content-derived, so it is the same fact, and the local one carries
that repository's provenance, which is the evidence somebody would check.

### Turning them off

`--no-global` on a single recall, or `ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_GLOBAL_FACTS=1` for a
machine where repository answers must not be influenced by anything outside the
repository. The variable is fail-closed like the other guards: an unrecognised
value disables global facts rather than leaving them on.

### Outside a repository

`remember` used to fail outside a checkout. It now records the fact globally and
says so:

```
not in a repository, so this was remembered globally; it will be recalled from every repo
```

This is decided by asking git whether the directory is a working tree, not by
whether a path resolves — any existing directory resolves, and the branch then
defaults to `main`, which would file the fact against a repository that does not
exist. Passing `--branch` still requires a repository: that names a specific
branch, and filing it globally would be a different write than the one asked for.

### What a global fact does not have

A commit anchor. There is no repository to cite, and an anchor pointing at
whatever happened to be checked out would be worse than none — `verify` would
resolve it and report the fact as evidenced by a commit it has nothing to do
with. `--global` and `--branch` cannot be combined for the same reason.

Note that multi-repository *code* analysis is a separate feature: see
`entire brain workspace` for brains spanning several repositories at once.

"""

p.write_text(s.replace(anchor2, section2 + anchor2, 1))

- "We deploy on Thursdays"


- **Global facts are excluded from the repository's semantic cache**, which is keyed by `(brainDir, branch)`. Retaining them would file their vectors under one repo's key and prune them from every other repo's view on the next recall.

input.content:
# Scale: how big a brain gets, and how fast it answers

Brain's row in every large-codebase comparison read **Unknown**, in both
columns, because nothing had measured it. This is that measurement, and the
command that produces it.

```sh
entire brain bench scale [path] [--json]
```

It reports index size on disk and query latency against a repository's size in
lines — the terms those comparisons are stated in — building the index in an
isolated store so it neither reads nor disturbs the brain you actually use.

**The headline is not flattering, and that is the point of publishing it.**

## Measured results

Apple M-series laptop, macOS, `syntax-only` profile, entire-graph
`v0.4.1-nightly.202609180615`, 8 fixed natural-language queries, 5 timed runs
each after one untimed warm-up. Every figure below came from running the command
above; nothing is estimated.

| Repository | kLOC | Files | Symbols | Index | KB / kLOC | Index vs source | Build | Throughput | Peak RSS |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| entire-api | 174 | 746 | 12.6k | 40 MB | 237 | 585% | 7.2s | 24k lines/s | 41 MB |
| entire.io | 485 | 1,835 | 29.1k | 103 MB | 218 | 655% | 22.7s | 21k lines/s | 48 MB |
| entiredb | 628 | 2,596 | 35.9k | 112 MB | 183 | 536% | 25.6s | 25k lines/s | 49 MB |
| entire-brain | 746 | 1,835 | 50.2k | 193 MB | 265 | 363% | 17.9s | 42k lines/s | 69 MB |

Code-search latency, against the semantic index:

| Repository | kLOC | p50 | p95 | p99 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| entire-api | 174 | 299 ms | 359 ms | 569 ms |
| entire.io | 485 | 1,329 ms | 1,701 ms | 1,777 ms |
| entiredb | 628 | 1,407 ms | 1,982 ms | 2,102 ms |
| entire-brain | 746 | 1,315 ms | 1,433 ms | 1,443 ms |

## What this says

**Index size grows roughly linearly with the codebase, at 180–265 KB per
thousand lines** — five to six times the size of the source it indexes.

**Query latency is already over a second at 500k lines.** It is not flat, and
between 174k and 485k lines it grows by more than 4x.

Against the numbers competitors publish:

| | Corpus | Index | Search |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Augment (published) | 100M lines | 250 MB | sub-200 ms |
| Zoekt (published) | ~2 GB, multi-repo | — | sub-50 ms |
| **Entire Brain (measured)** | **746k lines** | **193 MB** | **1,315 ms p50** |

At 2.5 KB per thousand lines, Augment's published index is roughly **100x
smaller per line** than ours. Linear extrapolation of our measurement to 100M
lines gives an index in the tens of terabytes, which is not a scaling limit so
much as a different architecture.

**So: Brain does not currently scale to a 100M-line codebase, and this is the
evidence.** That is a worse answer than "Unknown" reads, and a far more useful
one — it is a number to move rather than a question nobody had asked.

Those competitor figures are their published claims, not something we ran. They
are not measured here and should not be treated as verified.

## What is and is not being measured

**`code_search` is the number that matters for this question.** It runs against
the semantic index, which is the store that grows with the codebase.

**`knowledge_*` is a different corpus.** Facts, history and docs grow with how
much a team records, not with how much code there is, so their latency says
nothing about codebase scale. The benchmark reports how many records that corpus
holds beside the timing, because a sub-millisecond number over an empty store is
not a latency for anything. The first draft of this benchmark measured only that
corpus, found 0.4 ms, and would have published it as a large-codebase search
figure.

**The corpus denominator excludes what is not the codebase**: `vendor/`,
`node_modules/`, `third_party/`, `testdata/`, and binary assets. Counting them
would inflate the denominator and make every ratio here look better.

**Latency excludes process start.** One untimed warm-up runs per query, so these
are steady-state figures for a live process, not `time entire brain search`.
There is no process-level cache between searches: repeated identical queries in
one process do not get faster, which is why the numbers track index size.

## Reproducing it

```sh
git clone <repo> && cd <repo>
entire brain bench scale --json > result.json
```

The worktree must be clean — the indexer refuses uncommitted content — and the
repository must be a git repository, since the line count comes from
`git ls-files`.

`--repeats` changes the timed runs per query, `--query` replaces the query set,
and `--keep` leaves the isolated store behind for inspection.

## Limits of this measurement

- **One machine, one run each.** No variance is reported, so treat small
  differences between rows as noise. The 4x jump between 174k and 485k lines is
  well outside anything that could explain.
- **The largest repository tested is stated in the table and nothing is
  extrapolated beyond it.** A curve measured here says nothing certain about a
  codebase ten times larger; the comparison above is arithmetic on our measured
  per-line cost, offered as a bound, not a prediction.
- **`syntax-only` profile.** Richer profiles produce more relations and a larger
  index.
- **Languages the provider cannot parse contribute lines but no symbols**, which
  is why symbol counts do not track kLOC evenly across rows.
- The kubernetes measurement required re-initialising a shallow clone, because
  the provider emits an empty commit for shallow repositories and the indexer
  rejects the snapshot. The file content is unchanged; only the git history is.

Closes gap #16 on the feature matrix: *"Scales to 100M-line codebases — REAL GAP (unverified on our side). We have not measured Brain or Graph at that scale, so our cells are Unknown rather than a claim either way."*

## Turning Unknown into a number

Both our cells read `Unknown` because nothing had measured them. `bench semantic` already times indexing and counts symbols — but the claims in that row are about **index size on disk** and **query latency** ("100M lines in 250MB", "sub-200ms search"), and we could answer neither at any scale.

```sh
entire brain bench scale [path] [--json]
```

## The answer is no, and here is the evidence

| Repository | kLOC | Symbols | Index | KB/kLOC | Build | code p50 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| entire-api | 174 | 12.6k | 40 MB | 237 | 7.2s | 299 ms |
| entire.io | 485 | 29.1k | 103 MB | 218 | 22.7s | 1,329 ms |
| entiredb | 628 | 35.9k | 112 MB | 183 | 25.6s | 1,407 ms |
| entire-brain | 746 | 50.3k | 193 MB | 265 | 19.8s | 1,315 / 1,945 ms |
| **kubernetes** | **4,786** | **325.1k** | **1,171 MB** | **251** | **219s** | **12,294 ms** |

**Index size and query latency both grow linearly.** The per-line index cost is stable at 183–265 KB/kLOC from 174k lines to 4.8M — there is no sublinear behaviour to hope for. Latency goes 299 ms → 1.5 s → **12.3 s**.

| | Corpus | Index | Search |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Augment (published) | 100M lines | 250 MB | sub-200 ms |
| **Entire Brain (measured)** | **4.8M lines** | **1,171 MB** | **12,294 ms p50** |

Augment's published index is ~**100x smaller per line**; its published search is ~**60x faster on a corpus 20x larger**. Carrying our measured per-line cost to 100M lines gives a **24 GB index and a four-minute search**.

Brain is comfortable on a few hundred thousand lines and is not built for the largest monorepos. That is now in the README's Limitations, not only in a linked doc.

## Two measurement decisions that matter more than the code

**The first draft would have published a false number.** It timed `retrieveUnified`, got **0.4 ms**, and looked excellent — because that searches facts/history/docs, which were *empty* in the benchmark store and do not grow with the codebase at all. Code search now runs against the semantic index and is reported separately, with the record count of each corpus printed beside its timing so an empty-store number can never again be read as a large-codebase result.

**The corpus denominator excludes what is not the codebase** — `vendor/`, `node_modules/`, `third_party/`, `testdata/`, binary assets. Counting them would inflate the denominator and improve every ratio in the table.

Also fixed on the way: `retrievalMode` is an `int`, so `string(mode)` produced **blank column headings** with authoritative-looking numbers underneath.

## Honesty about the numbers

- **Variance is reported, not hidden.** entire-brain was run twice and differed by **48%**; the doc says to read orders of magnitude, not digits.
- **Nothing is extrapolated by the tool.** The 100M-line figures are explicitly arithmetic on our measured per-line cost, labelled as a bound rather than a run.
- **Competitor figures are their published claims**, not something we ran, and are labelled as unverified.
- The kubernetes clone had to be re-initialised: the provider emits an empty commit for shallow clones and the indexer rejects that snapshot. Content unchanged, history replaced — disclosed in the doc.

## Verification

**12 weakenings each turn a test red**: last-line-without-newline dropped, vendored code counted, binaries counted, symlinks double-counted, percentile off by one, mean dropping the slowest sample, modes rendered by int conversion, empty-corpus disclosure removed, run count fabricated, queries reduced to bare terms, byte rounding, `--repeats` validation.

Two initially did **not** fail, and both were my tests being too weak:
- a mode name of `"\x00"` is non-empty and unique, so it passed a blank check — now the name must be printable and identifier-shaped;
- the fabricated run count `5` equalled what the fixture expected — the fixture now uses 21 samples over 3 queries.

- `docs/feature-matrix.csv` untouched, as with the other gap PRs. This row should become a measured figure rather than `Unknown` in the consolidated update — and the honest score is that we lose it.

input.content:
# Benchmarks

Everything Brain measures about itself, what it found, and the commands to run
it yourself. Including the parts that go against us.

**What this page is not:** a head-to-head against another memory product. We
have not run one under conditions we would defend, and [saying so](#head-to-head-against-other-products)
is more useful than a number nobody can reproduce.

## Run it yourself

These cost nothing, need no API key, and work offline. They are the whole point
of this page: you should not have to take our numbers on trust.

```sh
entire brain bench scale        # index size and query latency vs codebase size
entire brain bench semantic     # indexing throughput and memory
entire brain facts eval         # retrieval quality on a generated task set
entire brain facts eval-compare # compare two retrieval arms
```

`--json` on any of them emits the full record.

## Scale: we lose this one

Measured across five repositories from 174k to 4.8M lines.

| Repository | kLOC | Index | KB/kLOC | code search p50 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| entire-api | 174 | 40 MB | 237 | 299 ms |
| entire.io | 485 | 103 MB | 218 | 1,329 ms |
| entiredb | 628 | 112 MB | 183 | 1,407 ms |
| entire-brain | 746 | 193 MB | 265 | 1,315 / 1,945 ms |
| kubernetes | 4,786 | 1,171 MB | 251 | 12,294 ms |

Index size and query latency both grow **linearly**. Augment publishes 100M
lines in 250 MB with sub-200 ms search; per line, that index is ~100x smaller
than ours. Carrying our measured cost to 100M lines gives a 24 GB index and a
four-minute search.

**Brain is built for repositories of a few hundred thousand lines and does not
scale to the largest monorepos.** Full method, variance and caveats in
[scale](scale.md).

## Retrieval quality: what moved the numbers

These are Brain measured against Brain — one retrieval arm against another on
the same corpus and task set. They are not comparisons with other products.

| Finding | Evidence | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BM25 over substring matching on history | 2.7x–5.1x useful/1k across strata, three repositories | BM25 is the no-embedder default |
| EmbeddingGemma fusion over BM25 | +13% useful/1k (t=7.08) and precision +0.016 (t=7.68) at 418k records / 2,584 tasks; replicated at +12.5% (t=5.09) on a second repo | Fused history arm ships, gated on a configured Gemma-class embedder |
| Semantic fusion on facts | +0.459 useful/1k (p=0.005, Holm-significant), precision +0.025, no token cost, n=121 | Fusion default-on for `recall` and `brief` |
| Locus-scoped retrieval | +59% useful/1k (p=0.027 raw, marginal under Holm), −112 tokens (p<0.001), recall −0.029 | Scoped retrieval shipped; outline kept as a map, not a ranker |

Full rows, task sets and corpus identities are in the [eval ledger](eval_ledger.md).

## Agent outcome: one proof-ready result

Retrieval metrics measure retrieval. Whether a brain changes what an agent
*does* is a different question, and a much harder one to answer honestly.

**One measurement has passed our proof gate.** A correctness task whose decided
value exists only in retained history, run four times per side:

| Condition | Validation pass rate |
| --- | ---: |
| no brain | **0 / 4** |
| full brain (history channel) | **4 / 4** |

`proof_ready=true` — the lift survives drop-one — with **0 hard integrity flags**
and 16/16 records provenance-backed. Without the brain the agent cannot recover
the exact decided value; with it, it reads it from history and restores it.

This flipped the history-channel correctness scope from no-claim to claimable.
It is one task on one repository with n=4 per side. It is the only agent-outcome
claim we make.

## What we deliberately do not claim

Brain's benchmark evidence runs under a **claim policy with an auditor that
refuses citations that have not earned them**. Most retained evidence sits in
`no_release_claim` mode on purpose:

```
claim_policy: no_release_claim
proof_ready_comparisons: 0
```

`mise run release:evidence` fails if a claim-bearing suite is not
provenance-complete, audit-clean, backed by a stable proof-ready comparison, and
run at least four times per side against the *current* task definitions.

So the MCP, Radar, codex-runner and efficiency scopes have numbers, and we do
not cite them. They have not passed the gate. The retained artifacts are kept
specifically so an auditor can see why they are not citable yet.

This is the honest reason nothing was published before — not that nothing was
measured, but that the bar for publishing had never been cleared.

## Closed negatives

Things we tried, measured, and dropped. A benchmark page with no losses on it
is a marketing page.

- **Query expansion.** An early d≈0.47 was an n≈8 artifact; at n=121 it
  collapsed to d=0.10, p=0.26. Stays opt-in.
- **Model2Vec fusion on history.** Significantly *worse* than BM25 on precision
  at production scale (t=−6.33 on 418k records, t=−2.84 on a second repo) with
  no useful/1k gain. A promising small-repo +31% was noise.
- **Conversation-exchange fusion.** Traded exact-match precision for one extra
  paraphrase hit. Ships dark behind a flag; `query` stays BM25-only.
- **RRF fusion-weight tuning.** Swept; every cell within noise. Equal weight,
  k0=60 stands.
- **Facts FTS5 BM25 as default.** Parity, not better (1.43 vs 1.50). Opt-in.
- **Scoped-floor via backfill facts.** Dead end.

## Head-to-head against other products

We have not run one.

A defensible head-to-head would need the same corpus, the same task set, the
same judge, and the same token accounting on both sides, with enough repetitions
to survive drop-one — the bar our own claim gate applies. Published numbers from
memory products are generally measured on their own corpora with their own
scorers, so quoting them side by side with ours would compare two different
experiments and call it a comparison.

What we can say from measurement rather than assertion:

- **On scale we lose**, and by how much is [above](#scale-we-lose-this-one).
- **Ingest is deterministic and uses no model**, so indexing cost is wall-clock
  and disk rather than tokens. `bench scale` reports both; there is no API bill
  to compare against.
- **Everything here runs locally**, so you can point our benchmarks at your own
  repository and get your numbers rather than ours.

If you are evaluating Brain against something else, the commands at the top of
this page run against your codebase in minutes. That is the comparison that
should decide it.

## Method notes

- Every number on this page came from a command in this repository. Nothing is
  estimated, and numbers that are arithmetic on a measurement rather than a
  measurement are labelled where they appear.
- Results are comparable only within a row's own baseline. Task sets, corpus
  snapshots and metrics differ between rows; the eval ledger states this and it
  applies here too.
- `useful/1k` is useful retrieved content per 1,000 tokens delivered — a
  quality-per-cost measure, so a result can improve precision and still lose on
  it by spending more context.

fix(mcp): hold the retrieval privacy lock across HTTP delivery too

The stdio loop seeds a privacy state on the request context and releases it only
after the JSON-RPC frame is on the wire. That ordering exists to close a real
window: a retrieval command checks its output against the exclusion state, and a
tombstone landing between that check and the client receiving the bytes would
deliver content that should already have been excluded.

The HTTP handler called handleMCPMessage with a bare request context. The tool
output buffer therefore saw a nil privacy state and took the immediate-unlock
path, so the window the stdio path closes was open on HTTP — under a comment
claiming "same dispatch as stdio", which is exactly how it went unnoticed.

Rather than repeat the ordering in the second transport, both now call
deliverMCPResponse. A transport gets the behaviour by dispatching through it
instead of by remembering to reproduce it, and a source-level test fails if
either file calls handleMCPMessage outside the helper — the defect was a call
site that looked correct in isolation and disagreed with the other transport,
which no behavioural test of either one alone would surface.

The delivery callback now receives the request context. That lets a transport
honour cancellation, and it makes the seeding observable: the first version of
the ordering test passed with the context seeding deleted, because it checked
only that a state had been created and not that it reached the context the tool
buffer reads.

4 weakenings each turn a test red: HTTP bypassing the helper, the lock released
before delivery, the lock leaked on a failed delivery, and the state never
seeded.

The result: a document whose extraction failed (encrypted PDF, scan, corrupt archive, oversized file) is still recorded in the durable seed manifest as `Extracted: true` with a `SeedPath` that was never written, and the "document not indexed" warning documented in `docs/reference.md` never surfaces. Pass `scan` by pointer through `writeSeedArtifacts` (or return the mutated value) so these corrections propagate.

fix(docs): carry extraction failures back to the caller and bound decompression

Three findings on the document ingest, all real.

writeSeedArtifacts took the scan BY VALUE, so the `&scan` handed to
writeSeedDocs mutated a local copy. Every correction extraction makes when a
document cannot be read — the cleared seed path, the reason, the appended
warning — was discarded on return. The durable manifest therefore recorded an
encrypted or scanned PDF as extracted, with a seed path that was never written,
and the "document not indexed" warning the reference documents never reached
anybody. My own test for that warning passed the whole time, because it called
writeSeedDocs directly and never went through the copy.

file-index.json is the documented place to see why a file was included or
skipped, and it was written before extraction was attempted — so it could only
ever report the optimistic answer. Documents are now written first, because
doing so is what discovers which of them are unreadable, and a document that
failed is marked not-included with its reason.

The PDF reader capped decompression per stream and not per document. A page tree
may hold thousands of pages; a page that inflates to the 32 MiB per-stream cap
and yields almost no text advances nothing that ends the loop, so a small file
could ask for hundreds of gigabytes of inflation. There is now a document-wide
allowance that the decoder spends from and refuses once gone.

6 weakenings turn a test red. Two early-outs deliberately do not have their own:
they short-circuit work the decoder already refuses, and the comments now say
so rather than implying a guard that is not load-bearing. The first version of
the budget test was also too weak to fail — its fixture never reached the limit
and it leaned on a timeout — so extraction now takes the budget as a parameter
and the test proves a small one stops the page loop early.

Delivery is synchronous, so it sits on the critical path of every command that
triggers it — and `remember` is called by agents, often. A five-second ceiling
on an endpoint that accepts the connection and then stalls made that command
feel broken, under a comment describing the call as fire and forget.

send moved to a goroutine is killed when the command returns — that is not fire

two seconds by default, enough for a local or same-region receiver, with

is not a positive duration falls back rather than disabling the bound, because a
zero deadline fails every delivery instantly and looks exactly like an
unreachable endpoint.

The comment now says delivery blocks, because it does.

Plus **#314** for the README install slop you flagged — that paragraph now says what the script does and what each flag is for, checked against `get-brain.sh`.

## Two matrix rows are factually wrong

- **Row 8 "Capture beyond a single repository" reads No/No** — but `entire brain workspace create|add|refresh|graph|impact|review` already exists (142KB of `workspace.go`). The real gap was facts having no scope outside a repo+branch; that's what #311 builds.
- **Row 16 should become a measured loss, not `Unknown`.** Measured across 5 repos to 4.8M lines: index and latency both grow **linearly** — 1.17 GB and **12.3s p50** on kubernetes, ~100x worse per line than Augment's published figure. Brain does not scale to 100M lines, and #312/#313 say so in the README and the benchmarks page.

Every gap PR deliberately left `feature-matrix.csv` alone — 12 PRs editing the same label-count table would conflict 12 ways. It needs one consolidated update.

## Findings: 29 dispositioned, 27 fixed, 2 refuted

The review posted 8 rounds. Real defects it caught, several of which were mine from the *previous* round:

- HTTP MCP didn't seed the privacy state, so the lock-until-delivered window stdio closes was **open on HTTP**; it also **executed JSON-RPC notifications** stdio ignores.
- Webhook delivery errors **printed the endpoint to stderr** — for Slack/Discord that URL *is* the credential.
- `writeSeedArtifacts` took the scan **by value**, silently discarding every extraction failure; my own test passed the whole time because it called the helper directly.
- Fact export wrote and deleted **through symlinked path components**.

The 2 I refuted: `--file` path traversal (reading a file the operator names is the flag's purpose — I ran the claimed exploit, it prints a parse error) and webhook SSRF (the URL has one source, an env var the operator sets; blocking loopback would break the local-receiver case).

**Round 8 just posted 3 more (2 medium, 1 low).** Findings per round went 11 → 5 → 4 → 2 → 3 → 2 → 2 → 3 — not converging to zero. Eleven rounds, **31 findings: 27 confirmed and fixed, 4 refuted.** It caught real defects, several of them mine from the previous round:

- HTTP MCP left the privacy window **open** that stdio closes, and **executed notifications** stdio ignores.
- Webhook errors **printed the endpoint to stderr** — for Slack that URL *is* the credential.
- `writeSeedArtifacts` took the scan **by value**, discarding every extraction failure; my own test passed throughout because it called the helper directly.

## Two gaps are losses, and #315 says so

**Scale** is now a measured loss, not `Unknown`: linear growth, **12.3 s p50 and 1.17 GB at 4.8M lines**, ~100x worse per line than Augment. **Published benchmarks** is `Partial` — the page exists with real numbers and the closed negatives, and it is still not a head-to-head, which it states in its second paragraph.

## What's yours

   - PDF internals: FlateDecode, `/ToUnicode` CMaps (bfchar/bfrange), Identity-H, content-stream text operators, PNG predictors

behavior, not the underlying source of truth.

## Global Facts

A fact normally belongs to a repository and a branch. That is right for a claim
about one codebase and wrong for the rest: "I prefer table-driven tests", "we
deploy on Thursdays", "the staging cluster is in eu-west-1" are true everywhere,
and recording them in one repo's brain makes them invisible from the next.

```sh
entire brain remember "We deploy on Thursdays." --global
entire brain facts global                     # list them
entire brain facts global --all --json
entire brain facts retract <fact-id> --global
```

Global facts live in their own store beside the per-repo ones — `global/` next
to `repos/` under the plugin data directory, which `entire brain facts global`
prints. They are ordinary facts: the same format, the same taxonomy, the same
retraction and garbage collection.

### How they surface

`recall` merges them into every repository's results. They go through the same
filters and ranking as repository facts, and are labelled:

```
fact:76aa6fd6 decision [architecture.deployment.convention] (global)
```

entire trail finding dismiss 227 01M345XGVMRDARE3GRRZKJ41X2 --repo gh/entireio/entire-brain -m "REFUTED — \`http.Server.Serve\` closes the listener itself, on every return path including the error one.

From the standard library's own contract for \`func (srv *Server) Serve(l net.Listener) error\`: *'Serve always returns a non-nil error and closes l.'* The implementation wraps the listener in a \`onceCloseListener\` and \`defer l.Close()\`s it, so the close happens whether Accept fails, the server is shut down, or the context path runs.

Executed rather than cited. An instrumented listener that counts Close calls, with Accept forced to fail permanently so Serve takes exactly the branch the finding names:

    Serve returned accept tcp 127.0.0.1:54229: use of closed network connection
    Close called on the listener 1 time(s)
    --- PASS

So the socket is released at line 252, not leaked until process exit.

The suggested remedy is also the one the finding itself flags as risky, and rightly: adding \`defer listener.Close()\` after :217 would make this a double close. It would be harmless in practice — \`onceCloseListener\` means Serve's close is idempotent and ours would return 'use of closed network connection' into a discarded error — but it would be dead code justified by a leak that does not exist, and it would read as though the close were load-bearing.

The \`ctx.Done()\` path is covered too: \`server.Shutdown\` closes the listeners, and the goroutine's \`Serve\` returns \`ErrServerClosed\` and closes there as well.

Probe removed after running; no production change warranted." 2>&1 | tail -2

retain and markTouched skip them, and factsVectorRanked keeps them out of
present so savePresent cannot write them. Global facts are still ranked
everywhere -- they are embedded per run, which costs one call and keeps the
repository's cache honest. recall, query/search/vsearch and brief now share that
one mechanism, and recall's manual filter is gone.

- **#308**: REST wrote search results under the *pre-ranking* privacy identity while every other surface uses the post-revalidation one. A cleanly-completed concurrent exclusion then made the write boundary refuse rows it had already filtered — surfacing as **HTTP 200 with an empty body**, because the status line is written before the body. - **#311**: merging global facts into the ranked set put them in front of per-repo semantic caches keyed by `(brainDir, branch)`. `recall`'s existing guard filtered only `retain` — but `factVector` caches *and* marks touched during ranking, so it was half a guard and copying it would have copied the hole. are steady-state figures for a live process, not `time entire brain search`.

one process do not get faster, which is why the numbers track index size.


repository must be a git repository, since the line count comes from
`git ls-files`.

`--repeats` changes the timed runs per query, `--query` replaces the query set,
and `--keep` leaves the isolated store behind for inspection.

**`bench scale <path>` was measuring the wrong repository.** `benchEnv` overrode the four plugin directories but never `RepoRoot`, and the query path resolves its repo from the environment (`runSemanticQuery` → `exportRepoDir` → `env.RepoRoot`, else `os.Getwd()`) rather than from an argument. So the documented `scale [path]` form indexed the repo you named and then timed queries against whichever repo your shell was in. The finding cited four precedents in this codebase that set `Env.RepoRoot` for exactly this reason; all four check out.

```

```

I've added a line to the docs saying which form produced the figures, because that distinction now matters to anyone reproducing them.

Had the runs used the `<path>` form, the 12.3 s p50 in `docs/scale.md`, `docs/benchmarks.md` and the matrix would all have been measuring an unrelated repository — the kind of thing that turns a published benchmark into a withdrawn one.

Everything else is pushed and green: all six branches that went BEHIND after #304 merged are merged forward, tested and pushed; `get` now resolves global fact ids; and on the two branches where a person was working the same findings, I took their work rather than overwriting it.

T226 01M35JMBD3CQ88D1TSBC12AJ77 [medium] internal/cli/facts_import.go:379
The retirement conflict detection at lines 377-381 only captures the first non-empty `SupersededBy` value for each fact ID. If two duplicate memories both have different non-empty `SupersededBy` values (e.g., memory A superseded by X, memory A superseded by Y), only the first is recorded in the `retirement` map, and the conflict between two different supersession targets goes undetected. The second duplicate's different supersession target is silently overwritten at line 392 without being counted as a conflict at line 390.
---
T230 01M35JME40QVNDTW735VDBB4SW [medium] internal/cli/docextract.go:431
In `extractOfficeText`, `budget -= len(raw)` only runs when the extracted text is non-empty (the `continue` on parse error or blank text skips it), while `readZipPart` is still called with the un-decremented `budget` as the read cap each iteration. A crafted `.docx`/`.pptx` with many parts (up to `maxExtractZipEntries` = 2048) that each decompress to near the 4 MiB cap but contain no `<w:t>`/`<a:t>` text can force repeated near-full-budget decompressions, defeating the aggregate output bound this budget variable is meant to enforce (contrast with the xlsx sheet loop below, which decrements budget before checking for empty text).

T230 01M35JME3FPH0RGHKTW34XE35P [high] internal/cli/docextract_pdf.go:289
`expandPDFObjectStreams` calls `pdfDecodeStream(objects, object)`, which passes a `nil` budget into `pdfDecodeStreamWithin`. A `nil` budget is unlimited per `pdfDecodeBudget.spend`'s doc comment, so ObjStm decompression during initial object scanning is entirely exempt from `maxPDFTotalDecodedBytes`. A PDF with many small, highly-compressible `/Type /ObjStm` objects (up to `maxPDFObjects` = 200000, each capped only per-stream at `maxPDFContentBytes` = 32 MiB) can force effectively unbounded aggregate decompression before any page is even walked — the exact decompression-bomb scenario the document-wide budget was introduced to prevent.

**mem0's 87.40 was mem0's bug, not mem0's quality.** Its adapter passed `limit` to
`search()`, whose signature is `search(query, *, top_k=20, **kwargs)` — `limit` was swallowed by
`**kwargs`, so every search silently returned **20 memories instead of 200**. We found it and
fixed it. mem0 gained **+6.04**. Fixed at `/app/main.py:351` in the mem0 container.

## The corrected result (2026-08-15, same window, both arms concurrent, n=1540)

`gpt-5.6-sol` as answerer AND judge for both, `top_k=200`, identical questions and corpora,
zero dropped questions, zero empty answers, zero failed judgments either side.

**We do not win every category, and the overall result is a tie.** Published as
"statistically tied; point estimate favours entire-graph", per a rule registered before the
numbers existed.

## The two numbers that make any sub-point claim meaningless

- **Noise floor 0.65pp.** Two *identical* mem0 runs scored 93.83 and 93.57, flipping 11.3% of

- **Paired deltas DECAY with n on this harness** — see [[paired-deltas-decay-with-n]]. Early

The shipped ranker admitted **one candidate per file** — right for code, wrong for prose. It
returned 19 results across 19 files while carrying 195 passages of evidence no `results[]`
consumer could reach, and 200 results carried only **19 distinct scores**. Two commits: promote
the discarded regions, then rank prose *sections* as independent candidates. 91.56 → 93.83
