from.content:
## What P5 delivers

Four capabilities, each one a thing teams currently do on instinct.

**Prompt intelligence.** Score a prompt's likely quality *before* it runs, from retained outcome signal. See which people write prompts that succeed. Curate a best-prompt library mined from real checkpoints, so the organisation's best prompting becomes everyone's floor rather than a thing a few people know.

**Fit modelling.** Which agent, model or person succeeds at which kind of task — from history instead of vibes. Today this is folklore: people know Claude is better at X and Codex at Y, and nobody can point at the evidence.

**Auto-routing.** Send work to the agent or person most likely to do it well, with the capability registry supplying the candidates. Fit modelling answers *who*; routing acts on it.

**Feedback loop and dashboards.** Outcomes flow back into the models, so the system improves with use rather than drifting. Leadership watches the organisation learn.

The milestones run Feb to Jun 2027: classifier, then per-person profiles and the prompt library, then the fit model, then routing, then the loop. **None of them has a scoped issue yet** — the roadmap lists them as "to be scoped". It is a direction, not a plan.

The origin matters for judging it: this came from the Salesforce ask. It is the part of the arc that someone outside asked for by name.

## Why brain, and not the four systems already here

Four systems already live in this space. The honest position is that brain is not obviously the winner on search — it wins on one specific thing.

| System | What it holds | Overlap with brain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| entirehq/mcp | ~60 tools over four upstreams, stores nothing | None — it is the transport brain should register on |
| librarian | Slack, Linear, GitHub, docs; pgvector, nomic-768 | The who-and-why half of team memory |
| entire-search | Checkpoint chunks, commits, PRs; Cohere-1536, Turbopuffer | Strips code before indexing; near-zero overlap |
| peregrine | Trigram lexical code search, tree-sitter symbols | Real duplication: two tree-sitter extractors |

That is four search systems, three embedding backbones and two extractors. Brain's claim is not "better search".

**What brain has that none of the others do: facts with provenance anchors tied to commits.**

A librarian document says a thing was discussed. A search hit says a string appears. A brain fact says *this decision was made, for this reason, in this session, on this commit, and it was later superseded by that one*. That is the structure a classifier needs to learn from — you cannot score a prompt's quality against a corpus that does not record whether the work succeeded.

The second thing brain brings is **eval discipline**. brain-bench already gates the extractor against a reference across ~30 languages and fails the build on drift. That pattern is the template for scoring a prompt-quality classifier, and it is the part most likely to be skipped by anyone building this fast.

So the argument is not that brain should own P5. It is that P5 needs provenance-anchored outcome data and a scoring discipline, and brain is where both already exist.

## The precondition nobody can code around

P5's hardest dependency is a conversation, not a milestone.

Alisha's MemoryRecords work — the Agent Improvement Engine — **mines the same checkpoint stream toward the same territory**, and owns the deployed semantic search that serves entire.io today. That is two seats at the table: the overlapping build and the production retrieval path.

The roadmap's own call is explicit: P5 starts with a merge-of-efforts conversation, not a third parallel build. The descriptive half (what happened) and the prescriptive half (what should happen next) are two halves of one problem, and the company currently has both being built separately.

**Treat this as a gate with the same weight as a technical one.** If it is skipped, the likely outcome is not failure but something worse: two systems that each half-work, mining the same data with different schemas, and a later migration nobody has budget for. The landscape already shows what that looks like — four search systems and three embedding backbones, which is exactly the cleanup P2 exists to do.

The cheapest version of this is a single meeting that answers three questions: who owns the outcome-signal schema, which system scores prompts, and whether brain's facts feed MemoryRecords or the reverse. None of that needs P1 merged or P2 defined.

from.content:
## Capture

Nothing works without this layer, and it is the one that fails silently.

Six Claude Code hooks fire during a session: `SessionStart`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `Stop`, `SessionEnd`. They write two transcripts — `full.jsonl`, raw and authoritative, and a compacted `transcript.jsonl` — plus checkpoints.

Checkpoints are git-native. Ephemeral ones land on a per-worktree shadow branch `entire/<HEAD:7>-<worktree:6>` so a session can rewind inside itself; persistent ones are condensed onto `entire/checkpoints/v1`. Session state lives in `.git/entire-sessions/`, shared across worktrees.

**The failure that matters.** Claude Code loads project settings from the directory the session was *launched* in. The capture hooks live in each repo's own `.claude/settings.json`. A session launched from a parent directory — a workspace holding several repos — loads no hooks at all, records nothing, and says nothing about it.

That is not hypothetical. It cost a four-day run here: 15 commits across three branches with **zero captured sessions**, noticed only when someone asked why the trails were empty. Meanwhile 66 sessions from another author were captured in the same window, because those ran inside the repo.

The second trap is adjacent. `init-agents` writes its guide to the **nearest** `.git` walking up from the working directory. Clone entire-brain inside your project, `cd` into it to build, and the next `init-agents` writes `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` into the clone — untracked by the outer repo, invisible to the team, no error.

Both now warn. Neither warning can recover a session that was never recorded.

## The instant core

Eight deterministic layers, **no agent tokens, about one second** on a small repository. This is the part that always works.

| Layer | What it builds |
| --- | --- |
| locate brain | Resolves the repo key and the store path |
| export sessions | Reads local checkpoint stores |
| seed baseline | Documents, entrypoints, commands |
| history index | Records, decisions, tool calls from git history |
| doc index | Chunks the repository's markdown |
| semantic index | Symbols and relations via Entire Graph |
| pattern layer | Recurring shapes across the corpus |
| memory coordinator | Ties the sources into one queryable view |

The store lives **outside the repository**, at `~/.local/share/entire/plugins/data/brain/repos/<repo-key>/`. That surprises people who go looking in `.entire/` and find nothing — I did it myself and briefly concluded zero facts existed when there were four.

The semantic layer comes from Entire Graph: tree-sitter parsing into symbols and a 30-type relation graph (CALLS, EXTENDS, IMPLEMENTS, DATA_FLOWS and so on), **with no vectors anywhere in the stack**. It is stored as SQLite under content-keyed generation directories, `semantic/generations/<commit>-<digest>/`, so a stale generation can never be mistaken for a current one.

Without Graph the semantic index is simply unavailable and the other five sources still work. Without captured sessions, brain falls back to code, docs and git history. Both degradations are reported rather than hidden — setup shows a skipped stage with its reason instead of a tick.

## Distill

The one step that calls a model, and the one that turns transcripts into knowledge.

It chunks each session transcript (48 KB by default), sends each chunk to an agent, and asks for durable facts as `kind<TAB>path<TAB>fact`. A reconcile pass then merges them against existing facts at the same taxonomy paths, retiring what is superseded.

It is agent-gated precisely because it spends tokens, which is why most repositories run with `facts=false` — of five core repos, exactly one had a distilled facts layer before this exercise.

**What the chunk size interacts with is not obvious, and three defects lived there.** A chunk must fit the model's loaded context window. Transcript text measures **3.65 chars/token**, and ollama loads many local models at `num_ctx: 32768`, so truncation begins near **116 KB** per chunk — and ollama truncates silently rather than erroring. The flag help used to recommend 128–192 KB, which is past that line.

A second limit: the per-chunk agent timeout was a hardcoded 10 minutes with no way to change it. A chunk the agent cannot finish in that budget fails, so a corpus of large transcripts crawls forward roughly one session per timeout. Both are fixed; the timeout is now `--timeout`.

The output is six kinds of fact. From a real run of 1,194:

| Kind | Count | What it captures |
| --- | --- | --- |
| decision | 638 | A choice made, with its reason |
| gotcha | 236 | A trap that cost someone time |
| invariant | 168 | Something that must stay true |
| closed-negative | 74 | A thing tried that did not work |
| convention | 50 | A pattern the project follows |
| preference | 19 | A soft rule |

**`closed-negative` is the kind that justifies the whole system.** Nothing else in the stack records what was *tried and rejected*, which is the knowledge an agent most reliably re-derives from scratch.

## What it costs, measured

From a full run over 203 sessions — 931 MB raw, 16.5 MB preprocessed, 482 chunks:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Instant core | ~1 second, zero tokens |
| Distill, full corpus | 17.4 hours on a local GPU, zero dollars |
| Facts produced | 1,194 across 16 branches |
| Coverage reached | 157 of 203 sessions |

**The cost is not uniform, and that is the part worth internalising.** Sessions process largest-first:

| Stage | Minutes/session | Facts/session |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Early | 4.4 | 1.3 |
| Late | 14–19 | ~19 |

The late transcripts cost about four times the time and yield about fifteen times the facts. The run finished at 4.4x the fact count projected from early sessions.

I produced four estimates during that run — 4h, 5–6h, 11–18h, 8h — and every one was too low, each time for the same reason: extrapolating from a window containing cached replays, which complete instantly. **Never estimate a distill from a window with cache hits in it.**

Running locally against ollama costs nothing but time. Against a paid API the same corpus is 482 extraction calls plus up to 482 reconcile calls. The local path is free; its limitation is that a 12B model holds the output contract poorly over long chunks, so a meaningful share of generated text is discarded for not matching the expected format.

from.content:
## What a fact is

A record with a content-addressed id, a taxonomy path, a kind, a status, a confidence and a provenance chain back to the session that produced it. Stored as NDJSON, one directory per branch.

Real examples from the 1,194-fact corpus, unedited:

> **closed-negative** `architecture.data.flow`
> *"A semantic floor for Model2Vec on history was tried and rejected: low-variance cosine scores on long prose (avg ~0.2) made it impossible to distinguish relevant content from noise; revisit only when a transformer-based embedder is used."*

> **gotcha** `constraints.invariants.general`
> *"Ollama GGUF backend silently truncates context at 32k; `num_ctx` must be set to avoid truncation."*

> **decision** `architecture.data.flow`
> *"The Truth/Index architecture (plain-text source of truth + derived SQLite index) was adopted so that index errors or schema changes are resolved via re-indexing rather than complex data migrations."*

The second one is worth dwelling on. That fact was already in the brain while I spent most of a day rediscovering the same truncation behaviour from scratch and fixing it. **The corpus contained the answer to the problem I was solving.** That is the entire value proposition in one incident, and it is also an indictment of retrieval — I had to be told to query before I did.

**A fact is evidence, not gospel.** Among the first four distilled, one contained a corrupted token: "Facts BM2S" where the source said BM25. Nothing downstream re-checks a distilled string against the transcript it came from. At 1,194 facts a small error rate is certain, so anything load-bearing gets verified against source.

## Branch scoping and provenance

**Facts are scoped to the branch the session ran on.** Sessions run on feature branches; agents mostly work on `main`. So the default view is frequently the empty one.

In the 1,194-fact corpus, 961 sat on `main` and 233 were spread across fifteen other branches. Early in that run the split was far worse: four facts total, all on `feat/stage1a-derived-index`, and `recall` on `main` returned nothing while telling me the corpus was exhausted.

That message has since been softened on main, but the structural point stands: **an empty recall proves nothing.** Check `status --json | .facts.branches` and retry with `--branch`.

There is an argument that `closed-negative` and `decision` should be cross-branch by default. A decision about retry policy is rarely a property of the branch it was discussed on, whereas a fact about a file's structure might be. Nobody has made that call.

**Provenance is what separates a fact from a search hit.** Each carries the session id that produced it, so a fact can be traced to the conversation and the commit it came from. That chain is what a prompt-quality classifier needs: to score a prompt you must connect it to what happened next, and only provenance does that.

The status field (`active`, `retired`, `superseded`) is how the corpus stays honest over time. Reconcile compares new facts against existing ones at the same taxonomy path and retires what no longer holds — though it compares against only the 50 most recent at a path, which was hit 19 times in the full run. Beyond that depth, supersession is approximate.

## The wire contract

A brain on one laptop helps one person. The north star needs a team's memory, which means a brain has to become a thing that can be shipped, verified and merged. That is the wire contract, and it is **merged and working** on the client side.

Four pieces, all on `main` in `internal/brainwire`:

**The manifest** describes an artifact and its sources, versioned major.minor with additive minors and tolerant readers, so an older reader can consume a newer artifact and ignore what it does not understand.

**Content addressing** means every reference is `RepoID + type + hash`. A fact set has one identity; two machines that computed the same set agree by construction rather than by comparison.

**Canonical encoding** guarantees the same logical content serialises to the same bytes everywhere. Without it, signing is meaningless — two encoders would produce two signatures for one fact.

**Manifest signing** signs the manifest rather than each fact, so one signature covers a whole artifact and the content addresses underneath make tampering with any part detectable.

On the server side the design adds per-object encryption with crypto-shred on retract (so a retracted fact becomes provably unreadable), fact-set advance under compare-and-swap on the branch head, and a tamper-evident hash-chained advance log.

**None of the server side is merged.** That is the subject of the last tab.

One design note worth keeping: the encryption exists because the current store would be one bucket shared across tenants. In-repo, or under a repository's own trust boundary, most of that need falls away — the crypto is a property of *where the data sits*, not of the data.

content.text: Now the Retrieval tab — where the value is actually won or lost:

from.content:
## Two disjoint surfaces

This is the single most useful thing to know about using brain, and nothing in the CLI tells you.

| Surface | Verbs | Searches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Prose | `query` `search` `vsearch` `recall` | facts, docs, history — **not code** |
| Symbols | `inspect search-graph` `inspect code` `inspect impact` | the code graph |
| Packet | `brief` | a task-shaped mix of both |

Searching a Go identifier through the prose surface returns markdown:

```
$ entire brain search "processMaxRSSBytes"
  seed/history-gaps.md

$ entire brain inspect search-graph processMaxRSSBytes
  processMaxRSSBytes   internal/cli/rss_getrusage.go
```

The split is defensible — facts are prose, code is structure, and one ranker over both would serve neither well. But it is undiscoverable: both surfaces answer, neither says "you asked the wrong one", and an empty prose result reads as absence rather than as a routing error.

**Practical rule: an identifier or symbol goes to `inspect search-graph`. An intent or a "why did we…" goes to `query` or `recall`.**

Worth noting that `inspect search-graph` found two symbols that Entire Graph's own intent-phrased search missed. The capability people assume is absent often exists under a different verb on a different tool — which is itself an argument for P2's single surface.

## What an agent actually does with it

The intended loop, which the agent guide installs as instructions:

1. **Before touching code**, `brain brief "<the task>"` returns a task-shaped packet: likely files to edit, likely tests, relevant prior decisions.
2. **To locate code**, `inspect search-graph` or Graph's search — not grep.
3. **To understand why**, `recall` for decisions and closed-negatives at the relevant taxonomy path.
4. **After learning something durable**, `brain remember` writes it back so the next session inherits it.

Step 4 is what makes memory compound rather than accumulate, and it is the step most often skipped.

**A worked example from this session.** Debugging why distill failed on large chunks, the honest sequence was: measure ollama's behaviour, find a context-window truncation, fix it, ship it. Total cost roughly a day.

The sequence that was available: `recall "ollama truncation"` returns, at rank 1, *"Ollama GGUF backend silently truncates context at 32k; `num_ctx` must be set to avoid truncation."* Total cost: one command.

I did not run it, because nothing in my loop made querying the default move. The guide says to; I was not following the guide. **That is the gap between the system working and the system being used**, and it is not solved by better retrieval — it is solved by the instruction being enforced rather than suggested. There is a built-but-unlaunched hook for exactly this: a PreToolUse gate that asks whether the graph was searched before a grep.

## Where retrieval fails

Measured, not guessed.

**Precision drops on indirect questions.** Asking *"why was FTS5 trigram rejected"* returned three `closed-negative` facts about entirely different rejections — identity probes, brief formats, a repetition threshold — and none about trigram. The query matched the *shape* of the question, not its subject.

The corpus has already diagnosed this itself. One of the facts it returned:

> *"Cap-tuning and semantic-reranking were tried to solve over-contextualization on the full-brain but failed; the issue is retrieval-relevance where topically-similar closed-negatives out-compete the decision fact."*

So the system contains an accurate description of its own failure mode, which says something good about fact quality and something uncomfortable about recall.

**Intent-phrased queries under-perform on the graph side too.** Of four test queries phrased by intent rather than identifier, one hit. The three misses were all phrased as *what the code does* rather than *what it is called* — and the agent guide explicitly instructs agents to query by intent, which is the shape that performs worst.

**Scale is a hard ceiling.** Latency and index size grow linearly: 1.17 GB and 12.3s p50 at 4.8M lines. A large monorepo cannot use this today. Five optimisation attempts produced one 1.83x win and four measured regressions; closing it needs an index redesign, not a patch.

None of these block the north star — a classifier mines facts in bulk rather than querying them one at a time. But they do cap the day-to-day value, and day-to-day value is what gets the corpus built in the first place.

from.content:
## What exists today

| Capability | State | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Local brain, all six sources | **Works** | 1,194 facts built and queried |
| Semantic index via Graph | **Works** | symbols + 30 relation types, no vectors |
| MCP surface, ~33 tools | **Works** | agents query it today |
| Distill to durable facts | **Works** | 17.4h for 203 sessions, $0 local |
| Wire contract, client side | **Merged** | `internal/brainwire` on `main` |
| Hosted store and sync, server | **Zero merged** | ~20 open PRs, no reviews |
| Remote MCP transport (M3) | **Not implemented** | no `brain/mcp` route on any branch |
| Web surface | **Does not exist** | zero in entire.io, and unscoped |
| P2 unified surface | **Not defined** | Linear issues all Canceled |
| P3, P4, P5 | **Not started** | gated |

The shape is consistent and worth naming plainly: **everything that runs on one machine works; nothing that makes it shared is merged.**

That is not a criticism of the work — the server code is written, tested and hardened. It is a statement about where the value currently stops. A brain that lives on one laptop delivers the single-developer benefit (which is real — the truncation fact would have saved a day) but none of the team benefit the north star is built on.

Fact coverage is also partial: 157 of 203 sessions distilled. The 46 remaining are the largest, which is why they time out, and they are likely the densest.

## What blocks the path

**Gate 1 — P1, the hosted brain. Blocked on review, not engineering.**

The server code exists: store, crypto, build pipeline, ref index, fact sync, Postgres sync, and three HTTP API layers, plus about ten post-audit hardening PRs. **Not one has a review.**

The cost of waiting compounds rather than holding still:

- `main` has moved **1,824 commits** past the stack's merge base
- one PR already **conflicts**
- one has **red CI**
- the umbrella PR's review gate is **erroring** on sandbox provisioning, so it cannot be reviewed even if someone started

And M3, the remote MCP transport, has **no implementation in entire-api at all** — verified three ways. The client calls an endpoint nothing serves. The real work is a separate open PR on the hosted MCP service.

**Gate 2 — P2, the unified surface. Not defined for this workstream.**

The roadmap's P2 exists only as Linear issues, all of which are Canceled. The only P2 in code is an explicitly non-mergeable RFC about code-search convergence — a different initiative. P2 also depends on other teams' systems, which makes it a poor critical path.

**Gate 3 — the MemoryRecords conversation.** Covered on the first tab. It is the one gate that cannot be unblocked by writing code.

There is a fourth constraint nobody has named as a gate but which behaves like one: **capture has to actually work.** Four days of sessions were lost here to a settings-resolution quirk, silently. A north star built on retained behaviour is only as good as the retention, and the retention currently fails without saying so.

## The shortest real route

Four moves, ordered by what unblocks what. Three can start this week and only one needs anybody's permission.

**1. Name an owner and a date for the P1 stack.** Nothing else on this page matters until that queue moves, and every week of delay adds conflicts. This is scheduling, not engineering. The gap-PR campaign is the proof it works: twelve of fourteen merged, zero open findings, nine review findings dispositioned — because somebody worked the queue.

**2. Prototype P5.M1 now, in parallel, gated on nothing.** The prompt-quality classifier mines checkpoints for outcome signal: success, iteration count, review outcomes. Those checkpoints exist today in volume. P1, P2 and P3 are needed to *act* on the scores at scale — auto-routing needs the registry and the surface — but not to *produce* them. This is the fastest way to learn whether the north star is real before paying for the arc.

**3. Have the MemoryRecords conversation.** One meeting, three questions: who owns the outcome-signal schema, which system scores prompts, and which direction facts flow. Cheap, and it gets more expensive the longer both builds continue.

**4. Ship P2.M3 as a thin facade; defer the convergence.** Define the unified MCP contract and route behind it to whichever engine answers best. Tools register against the facade; duplicates retire later without breaking a consumer. That converts P2 from a cross-team negotiation into something you control.

**What not to do:** skip the registration point. If P3, P4 and P5 each wire to whatever search they prefer, you add a fifth and sixth consumer to a landscape that already has four, and the convergence becomes permanently harder. The facade is cheap; skipping it is the expensive choice.

One honest caveat on the whole page. The north star rests on retained behaviour being complete enough to learn from, and today's retention is partial: 157 of 203 sessions distilled, capture silently absent for whole runs, and facts scoped to branches most queries never look at. **Fixing retention is less interesting than building the classifier, and it is the thing the classifier's accuracy will actually depend on.**

# Blocking

**2. `entire brain inspect impact --symbol ValidateToken`** *(Use Cases)*
**Errors: `unknown flag: --symbol`.** It's positional:
```bash
entire brain inspect impact ValidateToken
```

**3. The setup section never runs `init-agents`** *(Overview)*
`setup` + `status` only — so a CLI reader never writes `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md`. **This is the bug you reported.** It appears only in the Agent Prompt tab.

**4. `entire graph stats --repo`** *(Continuous Agent Memory)*
Errors without a value. Drop the flag entirely — it defaults to the current repo, and the trailing period in your sentence reads ambiguously as the argument.

**5. `entire/agent-guide.md`** *(Continuous Agent Memory, Brain section)*
Missing the leading dot. Source: `const Path = ".entire/agent-guide.md"`. The Graph section has it right.

# Corrections — I was partly wrong here

**6. The `query` vs `recall` examples** *(Overview and Use Cases)*
I earlier called `query` prose-only. That was imprecise — it's hybrid and nominally covers facts. But measured on a real 1,194-fact corpus:

- `query "ollama truncation context window"` → **four docs, zero facts**
- `recall` on the same question → **the exact fact at rank 1**

So both pages' decision examples (*"why did we choose this retry policy"*, *"why did we remove the queue abstraction"*) are pointed at the verb that in practice returns docs. Use `recall` for decisions, or show both. The Use Cases line *"Use `recall` for saved facts and `query` for a broader search"* is right in principle and misleading in practice.

# Missing, and users will hit these

**7. Facts are branch-scoped.** No page says so. An empty result on `main` proves nothing — 233 of my 1,194 facts sat on fifteen other branches. `recall --branch` exists and is undocumented.

**8. "From your repository's root" needs to be explicit** *(Overview)* — *"not from a cloned `entire-brain` directory."* `init-agents` walks to the **nearest** `.git`, and the build-from-source steps leave you inside the clone. That's your AGENTS.md trap.

**10. The daemon note could be concrete** *(Overview)* — it's a launchd service at `~/Library/LaunchAgents/`, restarts at login, polls every five minutes.

**11. The rerun instruction is prose, not a code block** *(Continuous Agent Memory)* — easy to miss, as you said.

## What it is right now

A memory layer that sits beside one repo on one machine.

Run `entire brain setup` and in about a second it builds six things, all deterministic and free: your captured agent sessions, a seed summary of the project, an index of git history, an index of your docs, a semantic index of the code (symbols plus a 30-type relation graph from Graph, no vectors anywhere), and a pattern layer.

Then there's one expensive step. `distill` reads your session transcripts, sends them to a model, and extracts **durable facts** — six kinds: decisions, gotchas, invariants, closed-negatives, conventions, preferences. On our own repo that produced 1,194 facts.

The `closed-negative` kind is the one that justifies the whole thing. Nothing else you have records *what was tried and rejected*, which is precisely the knowledge agents re-derive from scratch every time.

Any agent reads it over MCP — Claude Code, Codex, whatever — so the memory outlives the agent that made it.

**Concretely, what that buys you today:** this session, I spent most of a day discovering that ollama silently truncates at 32k tokens, then fixed it. The brain already contained the fact, verbatim, and `recall` returns it at rank 1. One command would have replaced a day. That's the product in one incident.

## What it will be

The arc has five phases. Today is the end of phase zero.

**P1 — shared.** Lift it off the laptop. One person's agent learns something; everyone's agent can read it. Content-addressed, signed, synced under compare-and-swap, authz'd per repo.

**Keystone — tied to git history.** Ask "which checkpoints changed `ValidateToken`" and get an answer from an index rather than a re-parse.

**P2 — one surface.** Right now there are four search systems and three embedding backbones in the company. P2 collapses that to one MCP tool every agent queries.

**P3 — agents stop colliding.** An agent claims a *symbol*, not a file. Two agents touching the same function get warned **before** merge. Handovers become structured data the next agent auto-loads.

**P4 — across repos.** Working in repo A surfaces relevant reasoning from repo B. Tasks route by declared capability.

**P5 — the north star.** Every prompt, session and outcome is already captured. Mine it: score a prompt's likely quality *before* it runs, learn which agent or person actually succeeds at which kind of task from history rather than vibes, and route work accordingly. The organisation's best prompting becomes everyone's floor instead of folklore.

## The honest gap between the two

**Everything that runs on one machine works. Nothing that makes it shared is merged.**

The P1 server code is written, tested and hardened — and sits in about twenty open PRs with **zero reviews**, now 1,824 commits behind main, one conflicting, one with red CI. It's a scheduling problem, not an engineering one.

The web app shows nothing of brain, and that isn't late — it was never scoped. P2 isn't defined for this workstream and its tracking issues are all cancelled. P3/P4/P5 are gated behind both.

One thing worth knowing because it's unglamorous and load-bearing: the whole north star rests on retained behaviour being complete enough to learn from. Today retention is partial — 157 of 203 sessions distilled, capture silently absent for entire runs if you launch from the wrong directory, and facts scoped to branches most queries never check. Fixing that is less interesting than building the classifier, and it's what the classifier's accuracy will actually depend on.

**The one-line version:** today it's a very good project notebook your agent can read; the plan is for it to become the organisation's shared judgement.

I couldn't read RFD-031 — five routes tried. `entire trail show` works with the `et/` prefix (not `gh/`), but the file itself needs the repo cloned and neither the remote helper nor HTTPS resolves it for me.

What I did get: **RFD-031 "Entire Semantic", by evisdren, opened 28 Sep, status open / phase building**, body pointing at `engineering/rfds/rfd-031-entire-semantic.md`.

That's suggestive — Evis owns **peregrine**, and the roadmap names exactly one real duplication in the landscape: *"entire-sem and peregrine both maintain per-language tree-sitter extractors."* An RFD called "Entire Semantic" from that author is most likely the convergence proposal. **But that's inference, not reading** — paste the markdown and I'll give you the real answer.

---

# Kickoff draft

## North star: "Build the git forge for AI-native teams"

**What's strong:** it's concrete, it names a category people understand, and it's defensible — you actually have the git-native substrate (entiredb, checkpoints, signed refs) that nobody else building AI dev tools has.

**What's weak:** "forge" is where the work *lands*, and your differentiator is what happens *before* it lands. GitHub is a forge. The thing you have that GitHub doesn't is that agent work arrives with its reasoning attached.

Three sharper framings to test:

| Framing | Bet it makes |
|---|---|
| "The git forge for AI-native teams" | Platform play — the place agent work lives |
| "Git preserves change; we preserve **why**" | Memory play — the reasoning layer is the product |
| "Your team's judgement, available to every agent" | Intelligence play — P5 is the product, the rest is plumbing |

They imply different roadmaps. The first says ship the forge; the third says ship the classifier. Worth forcing the choice in the room rather than leaving all three live.

**Hypotheses worth writing down so they can be killed:**
1. Teams will pay for memory that outlives one agent session
2. Agents using shared memory measurably outperform agents without it
3. Capture-by-default is acceptable (privacy, cost, noise)
4. One memory layer can serve many agents better than each agent's native memory

Number 2 is the one with a hole in it right now — see October.

## Who is our customer

**Now:** teams already running multiple coding agents who feel the context loss. Concretely: someone who moved from Claude Code to Codex mid-task and had to re-explain the project. Small, technical, early-adopter.

**Later:** the org buyer. Engineering leadership who want to know which prompts, people and agents actually produce good work. That's P5, and it's where the Salesforce ask came from.

The gap between them matters: **today's product is single-player, and the buyer is a team.** The hosted layer is what converts one to the other, and it has zero code merged.

## What are all-the-things

An honest inventory, since this is where duplication hides:

| | What it does | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| entire-graph | Symbols + 30 relation types, tree-sitter, no vectors | |
| entire-brain | Durable facts, sessions, history, docs | |
| peregrine | Trigram lexical code search, tree-sitter symbols | Evis |
| entire-search | Checkpoint/commit/PR search, Cohere + Turbopuffer | Alisha |
| librarian | Slack/Linear/GitHub knowledge, pgvector | Alex |
| entirehq/mcp | Hosted MCP transport, ~60 tools | James |
| MemoryRecords | Agent improvement from checkpoints | Alisha |

**That's four search systems, three embedding backbones and two tree-sitter extractors.** RFD-031 is almost certainly about the last of those.

## October: graph + brain hosted

This is the one where I have verified data, and the news is specific.

**The engineering is done. The merging is not.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Brain client (wire contract, signing, sync) | **Merged** |
| Brain server (store, crypto, fact sync, HTTP API) | **~20 open PRs, zero reviews** |
| Drift | main is **1,824 commits** past the stack's merge base |
| State | one PR conflicts, one has red CI, the umbrella's review gate is *erroring* |
| **M3 remote MCP** | **No implementation in entire-api at all** — verified three ways |

That last line is the one to surface in the room. The brain client calls `POST /repos/{id}/brain/mcp` and **nothing serves it**. The real work is a separate open PR on entirehq/mcp (#41, open since 29 Aug). If October's deliverable is "hosted", M3 is the piece most likely to be assumed done.

**Realistic October asks:**
1. Name an owner and a date for the P1 review queue — this is scheduling, not engineering
2. Decide whether M3 lands in entire-api or on the hosted MCP service, and who builds it
3. Rebase the stack before the drift makes it a rewrite

**One thing I'd add to October that costs almost nothing:** prototype the P5 prompt-quality classifier. It mines checkpoints that already exist and is gated on none of the above. It's the cheapest way to test hypothesis 2 before paying for the whole arc.

## Longer-term sketch

P1 hosted → keystone (semantic index tied to git history) → P2 one surface → P3 agents stop colliding → P4 cross-repo → P5 behavioural intelligence.

Two things to say out loud:
- **P2 isn't defined** for this workstream and its tracking issues are all cancelled. If it's a real gate, it needs an owner; if it isn't, the roadmap should stop treating it as one.
- **P5 has a non-technical precondition** — MemoryRecords mines the same checkpoint stream toward the same goal. The roadmap's own call is a merge-of-efforts conversation before a third parallel build. That conversation is as real a dependency as any PR.

## How do we want to work

The data from this quarter points at one answer: **review capacity is the binding constraint, not engineering throughput.**

Evidence from two queues in the same repo. The gap-PR campaign: twelve of fourteen merged, zero open findings, nine review findings dispositioned — because someone worked it. The P1 stack: twenty PRs, zero reviews, six weeks, now conflicting.

Same engineers, same repo, opposite outcomes. The difference was whether anyone owned the queue.

Concrete proposals:
- A named reviewer per stack, with a date
- Stacked PRs get reviewed bottom-up on a clock, or they get rebased into one
- Treat "code written" as 50% done, not 90%

One cultural note worth the room's time: of nine agent-review findings raised against my work this quarter, **seven were real defects I would otherwise have shipped** — including one where I'd have broken cost accounting on the most expensive calls. The review loop is earning its cost. The problem is that human approval is the step nobody is scheduled for.

Checked, and the headline is that **the two halves aren't in the same state at all**:

| | Brain hosted | Graph hosted |
|---|---|---|
| Server code | **Written, ~20 PRs, zero merged** | **Does not exist** |
| In entire-api | Zero on main | Zero, no PRs |
| Challenge type | Merging and review | Greenfield design |

Those incidental "server"/"semantic" hits I found are help text and config, not hosted work. So October's deliverable is one half that's finished-but-stuck and one half that hasn't started.

## Brain hosted — the challenges are mostly not engineering

**1. Review capacity.** Twenty PRs, zero reviews, six weeks. This is the whole thing. Same team cleared fourteen gap PRs in the same repo during the same period — the difference was that someone owned the queue.

**2. Drift compounds while it waits.** main is **1,824 commits** past the stack's merge base. #750 already conflicts. #928's CI is red. This gets worse monotonically; at some point rebase becomes rewrite.

**3. The review gate itself is broken.** #242's Entire Gates reports *"Findings: error — sandbox provisioning failed."* It can't be reviewed even if someone started today. Fix that first or the queue can't move.

**4. The stack shape forces serialisation.** #242's base is `m4-brain-9-proposals-api`, not main. Ten PRs based on each other must merge bottom-up, so one stalled review blocks everything above it.

**5. M3 doesn't exist.** The biggest risk, because it looks done. The brain client calls `POST /repos/{id}/brain/mcp`; **nothing implements it** — no route on any branch, no `brainquery` package anywhere. I verified three ways. The actual work is `entirehq/mcp #41`, a separate repo, open since 29 Aug. If October says "hosted" and nobody owns M3, you ship a client calling a 404.

**6. The wire contract has already drifted once.** PR #928 is literally *"accept the brain client's request bodies instead of 422ing"*. Client and server are in different repos with no shared schema check in CI. It will drift again.

**7. Storage direction is unsettled.** It rides session-share's S3 + KMS today because that was fastest; the stated target is EntireDB (objstore for blobs, refstore for the fact CAS, rsl for the audit log). The one thing EntireDB doesn't cover is per-object encryption with crypto-shred — which only matters because the store is shared across tenants. Shipping on S3 means migrating later.

**8. Correctness-critical bits that need real review, not a rubber stamp.** Fact advance is compare-and-swap on the branch head with 412 on a lost race and a hash-chained tamper-evident log. Tenancy is an injective `slug@ULID` across an org/project/repo SpiceDB cascade with two fail-closed layers. These are exactly the things a tired reviewer waves through.

## Graph hosted — different problem entirely

**1. Scale is a known blocker, and hosting makes it the main one.** Measured: **1.17 GB and 12.3s p50 at 4.8M lines**, growing *linearly*. On a laptop that's an annoyance; as a hosted per-repo index it's a storage and latency budget. Five optimisation attempts produced one 1.83× win and four regressions — closing it needs an index redesign.

**2. What do you retain?** The index is content-keyed per commit (`semantic/generations/<commit>-<digest>/`). Hosting forces a retention decision: every commit, branch tips only, last N? Each answer is a different storage curve.

**3. Who parses?** Client pushes an index, or server pulls and parses? Server-side means running tree-sitter across 30 languages at platform scale — which is a service nobody has built.

**4. The duplication is unresolved.** peregrine already does "one index file per repo on S3" at platform scale, with a tree-sitter symbol layer. Two extractors, and peregrine reserved explicit extension slots for a higher-precision external symbol producer. **This is almost certainly what RFD-031 addresses** — which is why I'd want it read before committing October scope.

**5. Freshness is harder hosted.** Locally I already hit `freshness: unsafe, branch_tip: stale`. Hosted multiplies it: whose commit is the index for, and what happens to a query against a branch the server hasn't indexed?

## Cross-cutting, and easy to forget

**Capture has to work or hosted brain shares nothing.** Four days of sessions were lost here to a settings-resolution quirk, silently — a session launched from a parent directory records nothing and says nothing. Hosting an empty brain is still empty.

**Someone pays for distill.** It's the only step that spends tokens. Local it's free-but-slow; hosted, the cost becomes central and needs a budget and a policy.

**Egress and residency.** Distill sends session content to a model provider, and hosted sharing adds "whose data crosses which boundary". There's an opt-in egress ADR for this, but it's a policy question that needs an owner, not a flag.

## If I had to pick three for the meeting

1. **Unblock the review queue** — name an owner, a date, and fix the erroring gate. Nothing else matters until this moves.
2. **Decide who owns M3 and where it lives.** It's the gap most likely to be assumed closed.
3. **Read RFD-031 before scoping graph hosted.** If it proposes convergence with peregrine, "graph hosted" may be the wrong October deliverable entirely.

content.text:
Found it — the **"What to ask"** table at **line 124 of a 362-line README**, so roughly a third of the way down, below Install and Activate. Joseph's read is right: it's the clearest value statement and almost nobody scrolls to it.

Here's the full accounting.

## Top part — fixed, in PR #321

| His report | Status |
|---|---|
| Stalled at 75/237, `--agent codex`/`claude` made no difference, doctor "pushed to 76" after 10 min | **Fixed.** Root cause was a hardcoded 10-minute per-chunk timeout with no flag. Each oversized chunk burned the full budget, so it advanced one session per timeout — the agent was never the limit. Added `--timeout`. |
| AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md landed in `entire-brain/`, not the repo | **Fixed.** `init-agents` walks to the *nearest* `.git`; his clone has its own. It now names both roots and prints the `--repo` invocation that targets the project. Reproduced exactly before fixing. |
| "typo on *so the snapshot is usabl…*" | **Diagnosed, not a typo.** It's a real message truncated mid-word by the display (`semantic.go:1783`). The bug is length, not spelling. **Not fixed.** |
| Rerun instruction buried in prose | **Doc fix, listed not applied.** |

Three tests, each verified red on revert. Suite green.

## Bottom part — he's right, and the answer is worse than Option 1 vs 2

**It's Option 2 (repo root).** The doc effectively says Option 1 because the build-from-source steps leave you cd'd inside `entire-brain`, and the next line says "start in a local Git repository" — which the clone *is*. His reading is the natural one.

**But the thing he found most confusing is the real bug: "my problem persists with Option 2 too."** I just verified why.

**`entire brain setup` never writes `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md`.** Only `init-agents` does — it's the sole caller of the installer — and **the docs' setup section never tells you to run it.** So from the repo root he'd correctly see nothing, and no amount of cd'ing fixes it.

So there are two independent causes, and my #321 warning only catches one. The other is purely a docs fix: **add `entire brain init-agents` to the setup section.**

## The new feedback — this is the most important of the three

**Joseph: agents default to known habits; without saying "Brain" it isn't consulted.**

He's right, and I can corroborate it from the inside: **I went an entire multi-day session in this repo without using brain or graph once**, despite the repo's own `.entire/graph-agent.md` saying *"SEARCH FIRST — never grep/find/cat to locate code before you have searched."* Every lookup was a grep. I only noticed when you called it out.

And the cost was concrete: I spent most of a day rediscovering that ollama silently truncates at 32k — a fact **already in the brain**, returned by `recall` at rank 1.

So two independent agents, in different repos, with the instructions installed, both defaulted to grep. That's not a prompt-wording problem, it's a **compliance** problem. Cole's "md thing that says you have to use it" is the same instinct and will have the same ceiling — instructions that merely *ask* get ignored under task pressure.

There is a built-but-unlaunched mechanism for exactly this: a **PreToolUse hook that intercepts grep and asks whether the graph was searched first**. That's enforcement rather than suggestion, and it's the only thing I'd expect to actually change the default.

Worth adding to the launch conversation, because "we shipped memory and agents didn't use it" is the failure mode that makes the whole thing look worthless.

**On the README restructure — I agree, with one amendment.** Lead with "What to ask" and drop column 3, as he says. But the two prompts in that table that map to decisions (*"Why did we remove the queue abstraction?"*) currently point at `query`, and I measured `query` returning **four docs and zero facts** on a question where `recall` finds the fact at rank 1. If you're promoting that table to the top of the launch, fix the verb first — it's the first thing anyone will try.

# Brain + Graph v1 readiness

## Context

Three streams of evidence converged this week:

1. **A user install report (Joseph)** — distill stalled at 75/237; `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` never
   appeared at repo level; doc ambiguity about where to run setup.
2. **Seven issues filed 2026-10-02** by two external testers (leine4550, peyton-alt).
3. **Two full agent transcripts** (Claude Code and Codex, same prompts, same repo) showing agents
   not using Brain or Graph.

Investigation of all three found that the headline problem is **not** that agents are habitual.
Three distinct, verified causes sit underneath it, and all are fixable.

**Already fixed and merged:** #316 (semantic memo on the wrong path, unbounded, unlinearized),
#317 (ollama envelope cap measuring the prompt, silent truncation, probe on an exhausted budget,
usage-accounting bypass, misleading flag help). **Open and green:** #306, #318, #320, #321.

This plan covers what is *not* taken care of.

---

## The three root causes

### 1. Brain's guide instructs agents to skip the tools

`internal/agentsetup/files.go:1-3` claims the package is "mirrored byte-for-byte in both
repositories". It is not. entire-graph carries directive text; entire-brain still carries a
permissive regression from 2026-09-14.

| entire-graph `guide.go:78-81` | entire-brain `guide.go:8-9`, `:31`, `:68` |
|---|---|
| "Your FIRST action … **MUST** be ONE Graph query" | "**Directly inspect source** when the task already provides sufficient locations" |
| "Do not skip the query on the grounds that the available context feels sufficient" | "**Skip ceremonial queries** for small edits and follow-up work" |
| | "Useful locations from the brief do not require a redundant Graph query" |

Claude's own transcript: *"The agent guide says to start substantive tasks with `entire brain
brief` and use Graph for code discovery. I skipped that."* It was following the guide it was given.

**`internal/agentsetup/coordination_test.go:137` and `scripts/test-agent-coordination.py:69`
actively ban the strings `"FIRST action"` and `"SEARCH FIRST"`.** The permissive wording is
enforced by CI. Graph's equivalent test comment says they are no longer banned.

Graph's guide (`guide.go:9-27`) states the measured cost: *"332 graph calls against 96,987
exploration calls (0.34%), and the graph-first rate was 0 in every session sampled."*

### 2. The tools punish the agent that does comply

From the Claude transcript, when finally instructed to run them:

| tool | result |
|---|---|
| `brain_status` | Error: 124,295 chars — exceeds maximum allowed tokens |
| `brain_brief` | Error: 125,822 chars — exceeds maximum allowed tokens |
| `brain_impact` | Error: 61,580 chars — exceeds maximum allowed tokens |
| `brain_entity_history` | `"matches": []` |
| `brain_regressions` | `"no code identifiers found"`, `scanned_files: 0` |

A context-saving tool that overflows context is worse than no tool. `mcp_response_budget.go:54`
exists but is only a byte-budget *notice*.

### 3. Warnings and failures are silently dropped

A sweep found four HIGH instances of the class that has already cost this project repeatedly.
Worst: `internal/cli/semantic.go:2380` — `FilterWarnings` drops any warning whose Detail merely
*contains* a `.brainignore` pattern, by substring with no path parse. This repo's `.brainignore`
line 1 is `entire-brain`, a substring of every absolute path in it, so **every index warning is
discarded** and status reports a clean index that silently missed files.

### Also confirmed

- **Codex could not use Brain at all** — `entire` does not expose `brain`; it found the local
  executable by accident. Packaging/discovery gap, separate from compliance.
- **entire-graph ships no MCP server.** In an MCP-first harness the "MUST run a Graph query"
  instruction names a tool the agent does not have. 37 `brain_*` tools exist; **zero** tool
  descriptions mention grep, "first", "instead of" or "before".
- **`hook pre-edit` already exists** (`internal/cli/hook_cmd.go`, shipped in merged PR #24) and
  **nothing wires it**. Not in any settings template, not emitted by `init-agents`.
- The nested `entire-brain/` clone degrades Graph's index:
  `W_GIT_WORKTREE_FALLBACK: nested .git marker at "entire-brain/.git"`.

---

## Decisions, and why

**Three stacked PRs, not one.** PR1 and PR2 both touch `semantic.go` and `distill_cmd.go`, so they
genuinely conflict — stacking is correct here rather than cosmetic. Risk to accept: a stall in PR1
blocks 2 and 3. Mitigation: PR1 is the smallest and most obviously correct.

**Guide text before enforcement hook.** The guide currently says the opposite of what we want;
changing text is free and addresses the cause. The hook is belt-and-braces and goes in the same
PR, but we measure the guide change on its own first so we learn which one worked.

**I will not unilaterally delete the test that bans directive wording.** Someone made brain
permissive deliberately on 2026-09-14 and defended it with a test. That may have been a response
to over-triggering. The plan flags this as needing the author's sign-off, not a silent reversal.

**Not in scope, recommended separately:** an MCP server for entire-graph. It is the structural
reason the Graph instruction is unenforceable in Claude Code, but it is a build, not a fix.

---

## PR 1 — Retrieval returns usable output and reports what it dropped

Bottom of the stack. Nothing above matters if the tools error or lie.

**MCP response budget**
- `internal/cli/mcp.go`, `internal/cli/mcp_response_budget.go` — enforce a real byte/token ceiling
  on every `brain_*` response, not a notice. Truncate with an explicit, machine-readable marker
  naming what was dropped and how to get it (`--json`, a path, a narrower query).
- Worst offenders to verify: `brain_status`, `brain_brief`, `brain_impact`.

**Status latency (#325)**
- `internal/cli/verify_cmd.go:833` → `:424`, `internal/cli/agent_surface.go:1053` —
  `populateBrainStatusVerification` runs `git for-each-ref --contains <commit>` per distinct anchor
  commit, a full reachability walk. Gate verification behind `--details`; keep the summary cheap.

**The four HIGH silent-failure sites**
- `semantic.go:2380`/`:2518` — `FilterWarnings` substring match against `.brainignore`. Parse paths;
  never match on Detail text. Report a dropped-count.
- `regression.go:316`/`:1224` — `SkipAll` at 20000 scanned / 400 seen with no warning, then prints
  "No suspected regressions (scanned N files)". Emit a cap warning; correct the claim.
- `export.go:3588`,`:3619`/`:382` — `usefulExportWarnings` drops `checkpoint snapshot unavailable:`
  unless `--debug`, and the reported `warnings: %d` counts the filtered set.
- `distill_cmd.go:79` `capWarnings` — cap of 50 applied *before* persisting to the manifest, so the
  dropped text exists nowhere. Persist all; cap only the display.

**Truncated user-facing messages** (`status_render.go:264`, `statusCauseWidth=140`, byte-based)
- `semantic_stream.go:518` (182 chars), `semantic.go:1783` (173, still unfixed on main),
  `semantic.go:6720` (147). Shorten the strings; make truncation rune-aware.

## PR 2 — Multi-agent safety, indexing, and Windows

**#326 — `brain brief` takes `.git/index.lock`**
- `internal/cli/git_harden.go:78-81` is the single git spawn point and injects no
  `--no-optional-locks`. Add it there; swap `git diff --shortstat HEAD` → `diff-index`.
  Call sites: `semantic.go:2613`,`:2617`,`:5022`, `agent_surface.go:4768`.

**#327 — indexing stalls on a dirty worktree**
- `semantic.go:575` + `refresh.go:795-796`: dirty && !`--worktree` → `dirty_worktree` error, and
  needs-rebuild returns true unconditionally on dirty, so every refresh hits the refusal.
  `watch.go:305-309` aborts the whole tick, so the cursor never advances. Index HEAD via a temp
  tree; let watch skip only the semantic step. Same shape at `seed.go:276`.

**#328 — Ollama is loopback-only and never auto-selected**
- `refresh.go:829-840` `defaultRefreshAgent` tries codex→claude→none with ollama absent;
  `distill_cmd.go:2349` rejects a non-loopback `ENTIRE_BRAIN_OLLAMA_URL` **silently**;
  `watch.go:110` hardcodes `"codex"`; `embed.go:300` repeats the pattern.
  Add an opt-in remote host, add ollama to the auto order, and **warn loudly when a configured URL
  is ignored** — silent fallback to a cloud agent is the privacy bug in the report.

**#322 — Windows "command line is too long"**
- `distill.go:137`, exec at `distill_cmd.go:2237`: argv ends `"--system-prompt", <7516-byte
  prompt>`, blowing cmd.exe's 8191 limit. The chunk is already on stdin. Move the prompt to stdin
  or a temp file. ~15 callers share `distillAgentCommandArgs` (`seed.go:1830`, `facts_eval`,
  `facts_write_cmd`, `pattern_*`) — fix at the shared builder.
- **Verification limit, stated up front:** I cannot run Windows here. The test asserts the prompt
  is not on argv and that total argv stays under 8191, which is deterministic on any platform.

**#324 — `facts promote --keep-both` queues confidence-0 proposals**
- `internal/factmerge/admin.go:128` emits `Proposal{Action: ActionSupersede, Confidence: 0}` as a
  literal, with no similarity ever computed, once per same-path target — quadratic fanout.
  Compute similarity, or do not queue when confidence is 0. Callers: `factsync/sync.go:118`,
  `facts_sync_cmd.go`, `facts_admin_cmd.go`.

## PR 3 — The guide, the hook, and discovery

**Restore directive wording in brain's guide**
- `internal/agentsetup/guide.go:8-9`,`:31`,`:68`,`:11-12` — align with entire-graph's text.
- `coordination_test.go:137` and `scripts/test-agent-coordination.py:69` ban `"FIRST action"` and
  `"SEARCH FIRST"`. **Raise with the author before changing; do not silently reverse.**

**#323 — the guide names a command that does not exist**
- `guide.go:33`,`:74`, `strict.go:66` hardcode `entire graph query`; entire-graph v0.4.0 dispatch
  has only `case "search"` (`query` lands in unreleased 0.5.0). Emit `search`, or probe
  `graph capabilities --json`. Same stale text at `docs/agent-coordination.md:107`.

**Wire the hook that already exists**
- `internal/cli/hook_cmd.go` (`hook pre-edit`, `hook post-failure`) is registered hidden at
  `root.go:169` and wired nowhere. Emit the `PreToolUse` wiring from `init-agents` so it lands in
  `.claude/settings.json` alongside the guide. Existing `PreToolUse` entries use
  `"matcher": "Agent"` only; this needs a Bash/Grep/Read matcher.

**MCP tool descriptions**
- `mcp.go:805-1030`, 37 tools. None say when to use the tool *instead of* grep. The description is
  what an agent reads when choosing; the guide is a file it may never open.

**In-repo docs**
- `README.md` — move the "What to ask" table (currently line 124 of 362) near the top and drop the
  Brain-command column, per Joseph's feedback. Fix its `query`→`recall` verbs for decision
  questions.
- `docs/agent-coordination.md:107` — stale `entire graph query`.

---

## Docs that are NOT in this repo

These live on the docs site, so they cannot be part of these PRs. They ship as a change list plus
an artifact (below), for whoever owns the site.

| Page | Fix |
|---|---|
| Continuous Agent Memory | **"up to 71%" is a retracted figure** — that instance had the graph arm silently falling back to grep on a zero-byte payload and a 452-word stripped baseline. Replace with cost +2.49% (CI [−6.83, +11.18]) or drop the number. |
| Continuous Agent Memory | `entire/agent-guide.md` → `.entire/agent-guide.md` (leading dot) |
| Continuous Agent Memory | `entire graph stats --repo` errors without a value — drop the flag |
| Continuous Agent Memory | Remove the `entire graph stats` recommendation (reported 82.9M saved vs an honest ~46k) |
| Continuous Agent Memory | The rerun instruction is prose; make it a code block |
| Overview | **Add `entire brain init-agents` to the setup section** — `setup` never writes AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md, which is why Joseph saw nothing even from the repo root |
| Overview | "From your repository's root" → "…not from a cloned `entire-brain` directory" |
| Overview | `query` → `recall` for the decision example; document that facts are branch-scoped |
| Overview + Use Cases | Copy fixes: "For example,you can move"; "lessons that **has**"; the run-on "…and make sure to commit…" |
| Use Cases | `inspect impact --symbol X` **errors** (`unknown flag: --symbol`) — it is positional |
| All | Confirm the "CLI 0.10.0 or later" floor; no version gate exists in brain's source |

**Deliverable:** a two-tab artifact — tab 1 every problem with evidence and severity, tab 2 the
corrected pages as they should read.

---

## Verification

Each fix gets a reproduction that fails before and passes after. Mutation-verified: patch the
guard, prove the test goes red (`verified-by-weakening`).

| Fix | Reproduction |
|---|---|
| MCP budget | Call `brain_status`/`brain_brief`/`brain_impact` against a large repo; assert every response is under the cap and carries a dropped-marker |
| #325 | Brain with ~250 facts; assert `status --json` under a wall-clock threshold; assert `--details` still verifies |
| FilterWarnings | `.brainignore` containing a string that is a substring of an absolute path; assert warnings survive |
| regression cap | Corpus over 20000 files; assert a cap warning appears and the "no regressions" claim is qualified |
| export/capWarnings | Assert dropped warnings are persisted and recoverable |
| #326 | Hold a `brain brief` while running `git status` concurrently; assert no lock error. Deterministic form: assert `--no-optional-locks` in the spawn args |
| #327 | Dirty worktree + commit + refresh; assert the index advances rather than refusing |
| #328 | Non-loopback `ENTIRE_BRAIN_OLLAMA_URL`; assert a loud warning, and that opt-in remote works |
| #322 | Assert the prompt is not on argv and total argv < 8191 (platform-independent) |
| #324 | `promote --keep-both` over same-path facts; assert no confidence-0 proposals and no quadratic fanout |
| Guide | Assert the generated guide contains the directive sentence and names only commands the installed graph exposes |

**Loop:** run the full `internal/...` suite under `-race` (CI runs `-race`; local darwin does not),
re-run each reproduction, repeat until two consecutive passes find nothing new. One suite at a
time — concurrent runs contend over the global brain data dir and produce false failures.

### The usage experiment (the deeper ask)

`entire graph stats` already computes a **graph-first rate**, and graph's guide records the
baseline: 0.34% of calls, graph-first rate 0 in every session sampled.

1. Measure the baseline on a repo with the current permissive guide.
2. Install the corrected guide. Run a fleet of subagents on real tasks (locate, impact, "why did
   we"), each in its own worktree.
3. Re-measure graph-first rate.
4. Then enable the hook and measure again — so we learn whether wording alone was enough.
5. Collect each agent's own account of why it did or did not reach for the tool. That self-report
   is what exposed cause #1; it is the highest-yield signal we have.

---

## Sequencing

1. PR 1 — retrieval correctness (smallest, most obviously right, unblocks the stack)
2. PR 2 — multi-agent safety, indexing, Windows
3. PR 3 — guide, hook, discovery, in-repo docs
4. Docs artifact for the off-repo pages
5. Usage experiment, reported with before/after graph-first rate

Nothing merges without approval.

## Open question for the author

Why was brain's guide made permissive on 2026-09-14, and why is the directive wording banned by a
test? If that was a deliberate response to over-triggering, PR 3's premise needs revisiting before
it lands.
