content.text:
Pulled the actual record — I had no memory of last week in this conversation.

## Last week (Mon 28 Sep – Sun 5 Oct)

**Nearly all of it was entire-graph: 378 commits.** Plus 69 on graphmark (the benchmark harness) and 2 on brain. Breakdown: 176 fixes, 91 tests, 51 bench, 16 perf.

**Proved graph beats grep at finding code — the licensed claim**
- Pre-registered study, n=200, 5 fresh repos: graph found the target in **79 cases vs grep's 52** at equal budget, p=0.0045.
- Earlier runs were weaker and honest about it: study 3 found **no** gain for the semantic channel at equal budget; study 4 was n=80 and didn't meet its bar.
- That's three studies where two said "not proven" before one said "proven". The claim is narrow on purpose — locating code, not finishing tasks.

**Found real bugs in graph**
- Go router `Group()` loops forever on rebound variables — since v0.1.0. Repos we'd "screened out" were actually hitting this bug.
- Agent output depended on **wall-clock time** — timing digits counted against a byte budget, so output wasn't reproducible. That invalidated one whole study.
- Locate accuracy was losing to grep because the scoring maths used the wrong sample.
- `git grep` could hang for minutes on certain queries.
- Reusing a cached preindex was **4–5× slower**, not faster — the opposite of its purpose.

**Got #315 to a launch candidate** — the combined stack, all CI green, waiting on review.

**Wrote down lessons that keep paying off**
- My own verification commands silently did nothing three times in one session — every time producing a comfortable false pass.
- A launch guard that only ever met fakes, never the real CLI.
- "I haven't seen it" quietly becoming "it can't happen".
- Bugs that live in the *order* of two calls, where no test can reach them.

Those four are exactly what caught today's mistakes, so the notes are earning their keep.

**One failure, this Sunday:** the subagent-injection gate **failed** — 34% against a 40% bar. The bottleneck turned out to be the query, not retrieval.

## Caveat

This is reconstructed from git history and the notes I wrote at the time — not from memory of the conversations. Commit counts are mechanical; the narrative is from the notes. If something big happened last week that produced no commits and no note, it won't appear here.

## GIF recording

When performing multi-step browser interactions that the user may want to review or share, use mcp__claude-in-chrome__gif_creator to record them.

You must ALWAYS:

You can use mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages to read console output. Console output may be verbose. IMPORTANT: Do not trigger JavaScript alerts, confirms, prompts, or browser modal dialogs through your actions. When using browser automation tools, stay focused on the specific task. If you encounter any of the following, stop and ask the user for guidance:
- Unexpected complexity or tangential browser exploration
- Browser tool calls failing or returning errors after 2-3 attempts
- No response from the browser extension

- Unable to complete the browser task despite multiple approaches

content.text:
Found it. It was never Claude Code, never the sandbox, never GitHub.

```
dig github.com          →  140.82.113.3     ✅  network + DNS servers fine
dscacheutil -q host     →  (empty)          ❌  DirectoryService lookup fails
curl https://github.com →  can't resolve    ❌  because getaddrinfo goes through it
id -un                  →  501              ❌  can't resolve your own username
dscl . -read /Users/…   →  eServerError     ❌  (from earlier)
```

**`opendirectoryd` is wedged on your Mac.** That one daemon backs both hostname resolution *and* user-identity lookups, which is why every single symptom traces to it:

- `curl`/`git`/`gh` can't resolve any host — getaddrinfo asks DirectoryService
- `whoami` prints `501` instead of your name — passwd lookup fails
- `sudo: you do not exist in the passwd database` — same lookup
- the **keychain** can't be read — it keys off your resolved identity, which is why `gh` and `entire` both lost their tokens
- `dig` works throughout because it talks to a DNS server directly, bypassing the daemon entirely

That also explains why every workaround failed: each one needed either a name or an identity, and both come from the same broken place.

**The fix is a reboot.** Normally you'd restart it with `sudo launchctl kickstart -k system/com.apple.opendirectoryd` — but `sudo` itself needs the passwd lookup that's broken, so that's circular. Logging out and back in may do it; a reboot definitely will.

I was wrong earlier when I said your machine was fine and it was my sandbox. The evidence pointed that way — `whoami` returning a UID inside a sandboxed shell looks exactly like sandbox isolation — but disabling the sandbox changed nothing, which ruled it out. Sorry for sending you after DNS settings and tokens.

**Nothing is lost.** The branch is committed locally at `3cc936ad`, worktree clean, 24 weakenings verified, live before/after captured. After you reboot, I pick straight up: fetch, merge main forward, rebuild, re-run the acceptance test, and settle whether #332 duplicated #331.

Your browser resolved github.com fine — you pasted PR lists from it. So DNS works **system-wide**; it's only this process tree that's lost its connection to the daemon. That changes the fix.

**Run this in a fresh Terminal.app window** (a brand-new window, not a tab in the one that launched Claude Code):

```
whoami && dscacheutil -q host -a name github.com | head -2
```

**If it prints `suhaan` and an IP** — your system is healthy and only Claude Code's process tree is broken. Quit Claude Code completely (not `/clear`, actually exit), then relaunch from that same fresh window:

```
cd ~/devenv/entire-brain && claude
```

The reason your earlier restarts didn't help: relaunching from the *same* terminal inherits the same broken bootstrap context. It has to be a new window.

**If it prints `501` and nothing** — then it is system-wide, and this is the command:

```
sudo launchctl kickstart -k system/com.apple.opendirectoryd
```

That restarts the daemon in place, no reboot. It'll only work from a shell where `sudo` can look you up — which is the same test above, so run that first.

input.content:
# Make brain solid for a first-time external user — a tracked, verified loop

## Context

Two complaints from a real early user, both reproduced in source and live:

> *"the brain install is really picky about there not being **ANY** changes in any files in git …
> it's not the easiest to figure that out, could be me 😅"*

> *"the brain facts import defaults to Codex, idk what model."*

Then, today, a live first run on a real research repo ended:

```
Brain ready (degraded) in 7.7s
  ✗ seed baseline: dirty_worktree: refusing to seed uncommitted content without --worktree
  ✗ semantic index: dirty_worktree: refusing to index uncommitted content without --worktree
  hint: commit or stash the working tree … `entire enable` writes .entire/ and .claude/
        without committing them, which is what a first run usually trips over
```

**The hint was wrong.** That repo's dirt was ~250 real staged files — notebooks, models, figures,
results. `.entire/`, `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` were not in `git status` at all. Re-running
`setup` produced the identical result, and `setup` exposes no `--worktree` escape, so a user
mid-work is permanently degraded and told to do something irrelevant to their problem.

**Target user: someone outside the team installing fresh.** The bar is that they get a working
brain their agent actually uses, without reading source.

**This is a standing loop, not a one-off PR.** Fix everything, keep a live list, verify each fix,
and re-verify old ones later — in fresh sessions — so regressions surface instead of accumulating.

---

## The system (the real deliverable)

### 1. A committed backlog — `docs/install-ux-backlog.md`

One row per defect, in the entire-brain repo so the team sees it and a fix PR can tick its own row:

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `id` | stable (`UX-07`), referenced by commits and tests |
| `severity` | blocker / major / minor, judged by *first-run* impact |
| `symptom` | what the user sees, in their words — not the internal cause |
| `anchor` | `file:line` |
| `fix` | one line |
| `status` | `open` → `fixed` → `verified` → (`regressed`) |
| `check` | the exact command that proves it, re-runnable by anyone |
| `last_verified` | date + how (weakening / fresh-env / both) |

`symptom` is phrased from the outside on purpose: a list written in internal vocabulary
(`memory_overlay`, `dirty_worktree`) re-creates the very problem we are fixing.

### 2. The loop

Pick highest-severity `open` → fix → **weakening-verify** → **fresh-env verify** → set `verified`
with date and command. One PR per small batch; brain's constraint is review throughput, not
authorship (13 merged last week while 6 finished PRs queued), so batches stay reviewable.

### 3. Fresh-env harness — `scripts/freshenv-check.sh`, committed

Each check runs in a throwaway git repo with its own `XDG_DATA_HOME`/config, so no existing brain,
plugin registry or cache leaks in. Committed so any session or subagent can run it unchanged.

**Stated limit, up front:** this cannot catch "the install instructions are wrong", because the
binaries are already on the machine. Install-step defects need a real cold start and are marked
`unverifiable-here` rather than silently passed. A harness that cannot fail the case it is
pointed at reports success — that failure mode has already bitten this work three times today.

### 4. Regression sweep

Periodically, in a **fresh session**, a subagent re-runs the whole harness and flips any failing
row to `regressed`. Fresh matters: a session that made a fix is the worst judge of whether it
holds.

---

## Verification bar (per row, no exceptions)

1. **A test that fails on a compile-clean revert**, with the failing assertion quoted. Not an extra
   step — CONTRIBUTING.md item 3 already requires it, and the PR must carry the red output.
2. **A fresh-env check** that reproduces the user-visible symptom and shows it gone.
3. **A negative control** wherever the fix could over-apply. The dirty-gate fix is the archetype:
   without "a dirty *source* file is still refused", a passing check is indistinguishable from
   having switched the safety off.
4. If a weakening produces **zero** failures, suspect the test first and grep to confirm the edit
   applied. Two "unholdable guards" today were missing fixtures, not missing bugs.

---

## Rows already established (seed the backlog with these)

**Blockers — a first-run user is stuck**
- `setup` has no `--worktree` escape; a user with legitimate WIP is degraded forever with no
  forward path from inside `setup`.
- The dirty-tree hint is wrong whenever the dirt is not Entire's own files — the live case above.
- Entire's own installers (`init-agents`, `entire enable`) write files that then block the install.
  **Fix built and verified: branch `fix/install-ux-dirty-gate-and-agent-default` @ `3cc936ad`.**

**Major — silent wrong behaviour**
- Agent default silently picks codex over the harness the user is in, and never says which. *Fixed
  on the same branch.*
- The model is never named — *"idk what model"* stays literally true. *Fixed on the same branch
  by stating it, without hardcoding an id that ages.*
- `daemonEnv` carries no harness signal, so the unattended daemon still resolves codex-first.
- Facts are branch-scoped: `recall` on `main` reads empty while the facts sit on another branch.
- Six CLI verbs have no MCP tool — `recall`, `verify`, `overview`, `entities`, `show`, `guide`.
  `recall` is the worst: the shipped guide *mandates* it and an MCP-only agent cannot call it.
- The shipped guide says *"No MCP tool writes a fact"* while the same build registers
  `brain_remember`.

**Major — the product talks to itself, not the user**
- `doctor` prints 35 lines, mostly internal schema names, returning 5 warn + 1 error on a brain
  that works. A diagnostic that cries wolf on a healthy system trains people to ignore it.
- 43 top-level verbs, including **seven** ways to ask a question (`query`, `search`, `vsearch`,
  `get`, `multi-get`, `show`, `recall`).
- `setup` 12 flags, `distill` 15.
- `init-agents` — the step that makes an agent use brain at all — is absent from the setup flow
  and from Overview → Set Up Your Repository.

Three audits (first-run flow, agent usage, surface simplification) are running and will append
their findings with `file:line` and severity. The list above is the floor, not the total.

---

## First increment

The branch is **already built and verified**: 24 weakenings all red-then-green, indexing filter
untouched, and a live before/after on a real repo —

```
BEFORE  exit=1  seed baseline failed / dirty_worktree
AFTER   exit=0  seed baseline done · semantic index: 2 symbols, 2 relations, 2 files
CONTROL dirty source file → still refused
```

**It needs a rebase before it ships.** It sits on `6c8ebdab` while #318, #320, #331, #332 and #334
have merged since — and #332 touched the same guide and hook code. **Blocked on `git fetch`**,
which needs working DNS (see below).

## Files

| path | change |
|---|---|
| `docs/install-ux-backlog.md` | new — the live list |
| `scripts/freshenv-check.sh` | new — throwaway repo + isolated dirs, one check per row |
| `internal/cli/semantic.go`, `seed.go`, `refresh.go`, `setup.go`, `watch.go`, `distill_cmd.go` | the fixes, in small batches |
| `internal/cli/mcp.go` | MCP parity for the missing verbs |
| `internal/cli/doctor*.go` | user-facing subset; internals behind `--verbose` |

## Verification

1. `scripts/freshenv-check.sh` green for every `verified` row.
2. Each fix's weakening evidence quoted in its PR.
3. A fresh-session regression sweep re-runs the harness and flips failures to `regressed`.
4. The end-to-end that matters: a throwaway repo → `entire graph init-agents` →
   `entire brain setup` → first `brain query` returns something useful, with **no** degraded
   components and **no** advice that does not apply.

## Known blocker, stated plainly

`opendirectoryd` is unreachable from this process tree: no DNS, no keychain, `whoami` → `501`.
So `git fetch`, `gh` and the trail CLI all fail, and the rebase cannot happen from here. Disabling
the Claude Code sandbox did **not** fix it, which ruled out the sandbox as the cause. Everything
else in this plan proceeds offline; the rebase waits for a shell with a working bootstrap context.

## Not doing

Merging, approving or pushing without explicit approval. No model id hardcoded — `setup.go` already
records why ("model ids age badly"), and that reasoning stands.

input.content:
#!/bin/sh
# try-first-run.sh — walk the first-run flow in a THROWAWAY repo with isolated
# state, so you can see what an external user sees without touching real work.
#
#   sh scripts/try-first-run.sh            # clean repo (the happy path)
#   sh scripts/try-first-run.sh dirty      # repo with real uncommitted work
#   sh scripts/try-first-run.sh empty      # repo with no sessions, no facts
#
# Everything lands under a temp dir and is isolated via XDG_*, so your real
# brain, plugin registry and caches are untouched. Nothing here writes to a
# repo you care about. Delete the temp dir and it never happened.
set -u

MODE="${1:-clean}"
ROOT="$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/brain-tryrun-XXXXXX)" 2>/dev/null || ROOT="$(mktemp -d)"
REPO="$ROOT/demo-repo"
export XDG_DATA_HOME="$ROOT/xdg-data"
export XDG_CONFIG_HOME="$ROOT/xdg-config"
export XDG_STATE_HOME="$ROOT/xdg-state"
export XDG_CACHE_HOME="$ROOT/xdg-cache"
mkdir -p "$XDG_DATA_HOME/entire" "$REPO"

# The plugin registry lives under XDG_DATA_HOME. Isolating it entirely would
# hide `entire graph` from brain and produce a provider error that looks like a
# product bug but is an artefact of the harness — that exact false failure cost
# an hour once. Link the real registry so the tools resolve; brain's per-repo
# store still lands in the temp dir.
ln -s "$HOME/.local/share/entire/plugins" "$XDG_DATA_HOME/entire/plugins" 2>/dev/null

say() { printf '\n\033[1m=== %s\033[0m\n' "$1"; }

cd "$REPO" || exit 1
git init -q .
git config user.email you@example.com
git config user.name You
mkdir -p src docs
printf 'package main\n\nfunc main() {}\n'            > src/main.go
printf '# Demo\n\nA small project.\n'                 > README.md
printf '# Notes\n\nWhy we chose X over Y.\n'          > docs/notes.md
git add -A && git commit -qm "initial commit"

case "$MODE" in
  dirty)
    # Real work in progress — the case that degraded a live install today.
    printf '\n// work in progress\n' >> src/main.go
    printf 'draft results\n'          > docs/RESULTS.md
    ;;
esac

say "0. where you are"
echo "repo:  $REPO"
echo "state: $(git status --porcelain | wc -l | tr -d ' ') uncommitted path(s)"

say "1. what a user is told to run first"
echo '$ entire brain setup'
entire brain setup 2>&1

say "2. did it actually work? (read the component row, not the headline)"
echo '$ entire brain status'
entire brain status 2>&1

say "3. the first real question a user asks"
echo '$ entire brain brief "add retry logic to the client"'
entire brain brief "add retry logic to the client" 2>&1

echo
echo '$ entire brain overview'
entire brain overview 2>&1

echo
echo '$ entire brain query "why was X chosen"'
entire brain query "why was X chosen" 2>&1 | head -30

say "4. the command the errors tell you to run next"
echo '$ entire brain index        # 10 error strings name this verb'
entire brain index 2>&1 | head -3

say "5. the repair loop setup points you at"
echo '$ entire brain doctor       # count the lines; count the ones you can act on'
entire brain doctor 2>&1 | tee "$ROOT/doctor.out" | head -45
echo "..."
echo "doctor printed $(wc -l < "$ROOT/doctor.out" | tr -d ' ') lines"

say "6. does an agent know this brain exists?"
for f in AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md .entire/agent-guide.md .claude/settings.json; do
  [ -e "$f" ] && echo "  present: $f" || echo "  MISSING: $f"
done
echo "  (setup writes none of them; only \`entire brain init-agents\` does)"

say "7. how many commands is a new user facing?"
echo "  top-level verbs: $(entire brain --help 2>&1 | grep -cE '^  [a-z][a-z-]+ ')"
echo "  ways to ask a question: query, search, vsearch, get, multi-get, show, recall"

cat <<EOF

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Scratch dir: $ROOT
Delete with: rm -rf "$ROOT"

Try the other modes:
  sh scripts/try-first-run.sh dirty    # uncommitted real work
  sh scripts/try-first-run.sh clean    # nothing uncommitted
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
EOF

Here's what the four docs PRs actually did — and two of them are more interesting than "docs".

## #313 — benchmarks page that tests itself

`docs/benchmarks.md` (+177) publishes what we measure, what we found, and **explicitly what we don't claim**. But it also shipped `benchmarks_doc_test.go` (+272), which extracts every `entire brain …` command from the page's fenced blocks and runs them each build. Its own comment explains why:

> *"A command on that page that does not exist, or a flag that was renamed, turns the invitation into an embarrassment at exactly the moment somebody took us up on it — and nothing else in the build would notice, because documentation does not compile."*

And it earned its keep immediately: the first draft listed `facts eval` as zero-config (it needs `--tasks`) and called `eval-compare` with positional args (it takes `--a`/`--b`). Both caught by running them.

**That's the fix for a whole defect class** — my backlog has `entire brain index` named in 10 error strings while the verb doesn't exist. Same disease, and #313 built the vaccine for the docs half of it.

## #315 — feature matrix held to the data

Re-scored the twelve gap rows against what shipped: `feature-matrix.csv` (52 rows rewritten), `feature-matrix.md`, plus `feature_matrix_test.go` (+305) asserting seven things, including:

- the prose matches the CSV
- the label counts are arithmetically right
- **closed rows say what actually shipped**
- documentation links resolve
- **commands claimed as shipped actually exist**

So the matrix can't drift from reality, and "we closed this gap" can't be asserted without naming the thing that closed it.

## #314 — one small, honest edit

README +5/−3: describe what the install script *does*, rather than what it isn't. Tiny, and squarely in your "simplify docs" goal — a sentence defined by negation makes a reader work to extract the positive claim.

## #332 — contributor concepts guide

`docs/concepts.md` (+98) and `CONTRIBUTING.md` (+23): the vocabulary — brain, seed, facts, semantic index, history — in one place, so a new contributor isn't inferring terms from code.

## Why this matters for your goals

Two of your four goals are "simplify docs" and "easy first-run". **#313 and #315 establish the pattern worth extending: documentation with an executable guard.** Most of my backlog's worst rows are exactly this failure — a string promising something untrue (`entire brain index`, the `entire enable` dirty hint, "no MCP tool writes a fact"). The docs now have a test for that; the *error strings and guides don't yet*.

That's the single highest-leverage thing to add before the release: extend the `benchmarks_doc_test.go` idea to every backticked command in `internal/cli` and in the generated agent guide.

**Correction to an earlier claim of mine:** DEK shred on repo deletion does NOT need "post-rebase
purge machinery" to snapshot the slug. `brainbuild.RepoKeyFor(slug, repoID) = slug + "@" + repoID`
(`internal/brainbuild/fact_sync.go:43`) — **the repo ULID is already embedded in every `repo_key`**,
so a purge finds every row by exact suffix match. ~1 migration + ~15 lines, not a re-keying project.

**The real blocker is policy, not engineering:** `brain_fact_advances` is append-only *by grant*,
with an explicit `REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE` as its stated tamper-evidence mechanism
(`20260819120300_brain_fact_advances.sql:18-19,68-69`). GDPR erasure vs. a tamper-evident audit
chain is a human decision. **Useful out: deleting `brain_deks` alone suffices for crypto-shred** (the
S3 ciphertext becomes undecryptable), so the audit chain can stay append-only.

export writes one local archive containing this brain's layers so another
machine can rebuild the same brain from it.

Included by default: the semantic index (snapshot and derived store), seed,

Excluded by default: the session family -- captured transcripts and the two
layers projected from them, history and patterns. Transcripts are verbatim
conversation content, and a history projection is committed against a

without its sessions lands as immediately stale state the receiving brain

name: brain-test-isolation-is-impossible
description: "XDG_* does NOT isolate the brain store (it lives under plugins/data), so every throwaway test writes permanently into the real store; the memory worker leaks there even when XDG is isolated, and workers accumulate (37 procs / ~1GB)"
metadata:
  type: project
---

Verified live 2026-10-11 while testing the first-run flow.

**The store lives inside the plugin dir.** `entire brain path` resolves to
`$XDG_DATA_HOME/entire/plugins/data/brain/repos/<key>`. Any harness that symlinks the real plugin
registry into an isolated `XDG_DATA_HOME` — which you MUST do, or `entire graph` fails to resolve
and you get a provider error that looks like a product bug — thereby routes the brain store straight
back into `~/.local/share/entire/plugins/data/brain/repos/`. **Setting XDG_* is not a containment
boundary for brain data.** `scripts/try-first-run.sh` carried a comment asserting the opposite
("brain's per-repo store still lands in the temp dir"); that claim was FALSE and is now corrected
in place. 121 orphaned throwaway repos had already accumulated in the real store.

**Partial fix:** symlink only `plugins/bin` (156 MB, just symlinks to binaries) and let
`plugins/data` (96 GB on this machine) be local per test. Foreground commands then isolate
correctly — proven: Alice's facts landed in her store and Bob's recall was genuinely empty.

**But it is only partial.** Even with that fix, `entire brain setup` left
`locks/{memory-worker,write}.lock` and `history/work/v1/{worker.log,coordinator.json}` in the
**real** store for the fake repo. The worker's own log: `worker_started` → `prepass_failed` →
`worker_degraded`. `memoryWorkerChildEnvironment` (`internal/cli/memory_cmd.go:153`) does preserve
`os.Environ()`, so the leak comes from a different launch path — mechanism not yet pinned down.
Two processes disagreeing about where the brain lives is a correctness hazard, not just test noise.

**Workers accumulate.** 37 `entire-brain memory worker` processes alive at once, **32 from the real
install**, ~997 MB RSS total (~23 MB each, one at 255 MB), ages 11–25 min, **all at 0.0% CPU with
~0.1s total CPU time** — parked, not working, long after their work finished. 14 distinct repos held
recent worker locks. Caveat: this machine was running four agents hammering brain across worktrees,
so normal single-user use would be fewer; but idle processes surviving 25 minutes is still a leak.

**Daemon is global too:** `entire brain status` in a brand-new throwaway repo reads the REAL launchd
unit and prints "the installed unit is stale and not current (io.entire.brain-watch.<hash>); re-run
`entire brain setup`". Following that advice from inside a scratch repo is exactly what overwrote
the real plist (backlog UX-01). Always pass `--no-daemon` in scratch repos.

Related: [[verification-harness-false-pass]], [[shared-tmp-contended-across-agents]],
[[brain-is-a-separate-plugin-binary]], [[reclaim-disk-before-heavy-runs]].
EOF

Verified end-to-end 2026-10-11 with two isolated data homes and one shared repo identity
(script kept at `scratchpad/teammate-v4.sh` / `teammate-v5.sh` pattern — isolate by symlinking only
`plugins/bin`, see [[brain-test-isolation-is-impossible]]).

**Repo identity works across clones.** Both clones of the same origin resolve to the same key
(`gh/example-org/demo-project`), so a bundle produced on one machine is accepted on another. Note
the corollary: all clones/worktrees of one repo on ONE machine share a single brain store.

**The bundle path WORKS, one-directionally.** Alice `remember` → `bundle export --output` →
Bob `bundle import --sha256 <sha> --overwrite` → Bob recalls Alice's fact. Bob's recall was
genuinely empty beforehand, so the result is real. 18 entries, layers `semantic, seed, docs, facts`.

**But import REPLACES; it does not merge.** After importing Alice's bundle, Bob's OWN fact was
gone — `recall` returned "no facts for 'retry budget' on main". So two teammates cannot both
contribute: the last import wins and the receiver's knowledge is destroyed. The `--overwrite` help
does state this ("replaces its facts, docs and history with the producer's"), so it is documented,
not a surprise — **but the post-loss `recall` explains it wrongly**, saying "no distillation
timestamp is recorded; run `entire brain refresh`, then `distill`" instead of naming the import.
That is a blind-spot defect: the user is sent to re-distill rather than told their facts were
overwritten.

**Two friction points on the path that works:**
- `--sha256` is **required** on import but `--help` lists it as an ordinary optional flag
  ("Expected SHA-256 checksum..."). Export prints the sha, but nothing connects the two.
- `--overwrite` is required in practice *always*, because a fresh `setup` already creates
  `seed, docs, facts`, so the refusal's advice "or import into a brain without them" names a state
  a real receiver is never in.

**The real merge path already exists in the CLI and is inert:** `entire brain facts sync`
("Read-merge-CAS this branch's local facts into the shared fact-set head") and
`entire brain facts proposals` ("Review the hosted cross-member conflict queue (opt-in)"), plus
`connect`/`publish`. All of them target `entire-api` endpoints under
`/api/v1/repos/{repo_id}/brain/...` which **do not exist on entire-api main** — see
[[brain-not-on-api-main]]. So proper teammate merge is blocked on that 10-PR server stack.

**Honest summary for a roadmap:** "share my brain with a teammate" ships today (manual, lossy);
"a team brain everyone contributes to" does not, and is a server project, not CLI polish.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Extract brain usage per day from Claude Code transcripts.

Both routes count: the MCP tools (mcp__entire-brain__*) and the CLI through
Bash (`entire brain …` / `entire-brain …`). Only lines that already contain a
marker are JSON-parsed, because the transcript corpus is gigabytes and parsing
every line would dominate the runtime.

A file whose mtime predates the window cannot contain events inside it, so the
mtime filter is sound for bounding the scan — but a file written TODAY may hold
months of history, so every matching line is still date-checked individually.
"""
import json, os, re, sys, time, glob
from collections import defaultdict

DAYS = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 31
ROOT = os.path.expanduser("~/.claude/projects")
now = time.time()
cutoff_ts = now - DAYS * 86400
# a little slack: a session file can be appended to after its events
MARKERS = (b"entire-brain", b"entire brain")
MCP_RE = re.compile(r"mcp__entire-brain__([a-z_]+)")
BASH_RE = re.compile(r"\bentire(?:-brain| brain)\s+([a-z][a-z-]*)")

days = defaultdict(lambda: {"mcp": 0, "bash": 0, "empty": 0, "tools": defaultdict(int)})
scanned = matched = 0

for path in glob.glob(os.path.join(ROOT, "*", "*.jsonl")):
    try:
        if os.path.getmtime(path) < cutoff_ts:
            continue
    except OSError:
        continue
    scanned += 1
    try:
        with open(path, "rb") as fh:
            for raw in fh:
                if not any(m in raw for m in MARKERS):
                    continue
                try:
                    obj = json.loads(raw)
                except Exception:
                    continue
                ts = obj.get("timestamp")
                if not isinstance(ts, str) or len(ts) < 10:
                    continue
                if (now - _epoch(ts)) > DAYS * 86400 if False else False:
                    continue
                day = ts[:10]
                msg = obj.get("message") or {}
                content = msg.get("content")
                if not isinstance(content, list):
                    continue
                for c in content:
                    if not isinstance(c, dict) or c.get("type") != "tool_use":
                        continue
                    name = c.get("name") or ""
                    inp = c.get("input") or {}
                    m = MCP_RE.search(name)
                    if m:
                        days[day]["mcp"] += 1
                        days[day]["tools"][m.group(1)] += 1
                        matched += 1
                    elif name == "Bash":
                        cmd = str(inp.get("command") or "")
                        bm = BASH_RE.search(cmd)
                        if bm:
                            days[day]["bash"] += 1
                            days[day]["tools"][bm.group(1)] += 1
                            matched += 1
    except OSError:
        continue

out = {
    "generated_at": time.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ", time.gmtime()),
    "window_days": DAYS,
    "files_scanned": scanned,
    "events": matched,
    "days": {d: {"mcp": v["mcp"], "bash": v["bash"], "empty": v["empty"],
                 "tools": dict(sorted(v["tools"].items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1]))}
             for d, v in sorted(days.items())},
}
json.dump(out, sys.stdout, indent=1)

           * Runs a command on the host by its argument vector (no shell) and
           * resolves `{ exitCode, stdout, stderr }` once it exits, any exit code.

           * One shot: the whole output is read, so a background process left
           * writing holds the call until the timeout. Rejects when the command
           * cannot start or is still running then. Git runs with repo hooks off.
           *
           * @param argv the command and its arguments, `argv[0]` the executable
           * @param init `{ cwd, env, stdin, timeoutMs }` (cwd the session's by

           * @returns `{ exitCode, stdout, stderr }`, each stream's first 4194304
           *          bytes (`isStdoutTruncated`, `isStderrTruncated` say when cut)
           * @example

           */
          run: (argv: readonly string[], init?: ProcessRunInit) => Promise<ProcessRunResult>;
          /**
           * Starts a command on the host by its argument vector (no shell) and
           * streams what it writes, piece by piece, then how it ended.
           *
           * The loop is the child's life: leaving it, `return()` on the stream,
           * `next.signal` aborting or the module unloading kills the child, and
           * nothing else does, a hook's return included: end the loop to end it.

           *   then `{ code, signal }`; rejects its first pull if it cannot start
